family-q1-f01.chunkText:
# Raceway and wiring methods

A family of practitioner questions in the Permissibility and compliance type (Q1). These patterns concern permitted cables, conduits, raceways, fittings, routing methods, and wiring-system transitions.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 245 (13.0% of all Permissibility and compliance questions)
- Never received any reply: 117 (47.8%)
- Replied but unresolved: 20
- Answered: 108 (answer rate among the 128 replied questions: 84.4%)
- Question activity by year: 2011: 1, 2012: 1, 2014: 1, 2015: 2, 2016: 1, 2017: 3, 2018: 1, 2019: 3, 2020: 16, 2021: 42, 2022: 64, 2023: 64, 2024: 37, 2025: 9
- Main subject categories: Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (183), Code Interpretation, Safety, and Field Operations (20), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (18)

## Common question patterns
- "Is metallic conduit permitted and suitable for carrying electrical conductors?" (asked by 7 commenters)
- "Is running NM cable outside the building inside conduit permitted in a damp or wet location under the NEC?" (asked by 7 commenters)
- "Is it permissible to remove NM cable sheathing and run the individual conductors in conduit?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Can NM cable be installed inside conduit?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Is using aluminum wiring permissible for service-entrance conductors?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Can PVC conduit be used instead of metal conduit or for this wiring installation?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Is installing the depicted conduit saddle permitted or used outside the post-Soviet regulatory space?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are low-voltage conductors permitted to be routed with power conductors?" (asked by 3 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Question when the cover breaks off can you only replace the front portion of box it does the entire box have to be replaced. You should show the NEC requirement of sealing all cables & wires transition from a warm to cold environment." (V:R672LpOdfcw) (Q:Ugw2qDPN-jGujtnKiZt4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Explanation): You can replace the LB cover without replacing the entire box. Seal cable/conductor penetrations with caulk/foam or gaskets per NEC 300.7(A) to prevent condensation and moisture ingress.

Q: "As someone with experience with this stuff, I would assume expanded polystyrene (EPS) is the insulation. I have seen when PVC coated cables are laid on EPS it eats into the cables and cause them to become very brittle. I can't see this bei…" (V:9P9_AieEFEI) (Q:UgzV4aCzmqEoRcgMvtx4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation, Prescription): One reply states that NM cable's outer sheath protects the inner conductors and that the electrical code permits routing NM in EPS channels, implying additional conduit may not be required.

Q: "358.30(A) EMT shall be securely fastened within (3 ft) of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, conduit body, or other tubing termination. Since you didnt make any box offsets this is not to code correct?" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:UgzQoQ_4qNLphQ8UNiZ4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Correction, Prescription): The consensus is that pipe or nail straps positioned within 3 ft of the box satisfy NEC 358.30(A); box offsets are not required for concealed installations provided the EMT is properly strapped.

Q: "I've seen electricians in Wisconsin use a single piece of 2" schedule 80 pvc to run ALL of the wires into the top of the box. Doesn't seem right to me but it sure made things easier for him and it passed inspection...." (V:LdNuJksviTY) (Q:UgxXjUq_73B7a86IpAV4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Correction, Explanation): The dominant reply states inspectors now disallow the single large conduit because of thermal issues and raceway overfill, i.e., a code violation cited at inspection.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "What would the requirements be for terminating the conduit where romex enter and leaves a run of conduit? Does there need to be a strain relief or some type of busihing?" (V:OeuWsYy6bvE) (Q:Ugy_6fcWgx9AOcxQ60h4AaABAg)

family-q1-f02.title: Grounding bonding and electrodes
family-q1-f02.chunkText:
# Grounding bonding and electrodes

A family of practitioner questions in the Permissibility and compliance type (Q1). These patterns concern grounding conductors, bonding hardware, grounding electrodes, earthing, and neutral-to-ground relationships.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 218 (11.5% of all Permissibility and compliance questions)
- Never received any reply: 87 (39.9%)
- Replied but unresolved: 22
- Answered: 109 (answer rate among the 131 replied questions: 83.2%)
- Question activity by year: 2019: 10, 2020: 13, 2021: 40, 2022: 35, 2023: 39, 2024: 49, 2025: 32
- Main subject categories: Grounding, Bonding, and Fault Management (125), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (58), Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (16)

## Common question patterns
- "Are neutral and equipment-grounding conductors required to be separated, with bonding permitted only at the service disconnect rather than downstream?" (asked by 22 commenters)
- "May neutral and equipment-grounding conductors be terminated or bonded on the same bus?" (asked by 12 commenters)
- "Are one or two grounding electrode rods required?" (asked by 11 commenters)
- "Is it permissible to connect the grounding conductor to the neutral conductor at the meter enclosure?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Must neutral and equipment grounding conductors use separate bars, or may they share a bar at the meter or main service panel?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Are grounding and bonding connections required or permitted at the main service equipment?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Does each detached subpanel require its own grounding electrode, or is the main service grounding electrode sufficient?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Is a bonding bushing or clamp required where service conductors enter the panel?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "I don’t get it, some videos say don’t run ground to neutral and some say it’s ok. So which is right? A main panel you can put ground and neutral together but a sub panel they need to be separate….why??" (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:Ugwv1AeiC8g0mkc0YiF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Per NEC practice, neutral-to-ground bonding is performed only at the main service disconnect; bonding at a subpanel creates a parallel return path, causing the equipment grounding conductor to carry neutral current and potentially energize grounding electrodes.

Q: "Is this a sub panel where you need to separate neutrals and grounds? I didn't catch if this was a main panel." (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:Ugzhg-021i3cqqDvmct4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The replies confirm this is a service/main panel where the neutral bus is bonded to the equipment grounding conductor and grounding electrode system. Subpanels, by contrast, require isolated neutrals and an EGC continuity path per NEC 250.

Q: "I like the free air ground.... that's code right?" (V:Jpu-3zB8Pqs) (Q:Ugzhjtv4Rd5UfHMdgUp4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Correction): Ground the metallic box and run an equipment grounding conductor with the circuit conductors; size the EGC based on the circuit's overcurrent protection device. Also ensure proper bonding and cable support near the box.

Q: "So do you keep running the ground back to the ground back to and from the ground post" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgySuWJUzwsKQGW0z_N4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Route continuous equipment grounding conductors (EGCs) back to the service/panel and splice all EGCs in each box, adding a pigtail to bond each device, per NEC grounding/bonding practice.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "Nice tutorial, can i ask a question, there are two screws next to each breaker, can i simply put the hot wire in the breaker the neutral in one screw and the ground next to it on the neutral buss bar? Or do all of the grounds have to be in…" (V:-nBDlutORiQ) (Q:UgzqwfYEYTjWZDWhMKV4AaABAg)

family-q1-f03.title: Boxes splices and terminations
family-q1-f03.chunkText:
# Boxes splices and terminations

A family of practitioner questions in the Permissibility and compliance type (Q1). These patterns concern electrical boxes, enclosures, splices, connectors, pigtails, terminals, and conductor-ending practices.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 202 (10.7% of all Permissibility and compliance questions)
- Never received any reply: 122 (60.4%)
- Replied but unresolved: 20
- Answered: 60 (answer rate among the 80 replied questions: 75.0%)
- Question activity by year: 2014: 1, 2018: 1, 2020: 10, 2021: 30, 2022: 65, 2023: 57, 2024: 31, 2025: 7
- Main subject categories: Other/Unmapped (117), Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (30), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (25)

## Common question patterns
- "Is anti-oxidation compound required or permitted on aluminum conductor terminations?" (asked by 26 commenters)
- "Are Wago connectors permitted for electrical splices, terminations, or pigtails?" (asked by 7 commenters)
- "Are aluminum conductors permitted for residential service or feeder wiring?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Are lever-type wire connectors permissible for residential branch-circuit splices?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Are junction-box covers required under the NEC?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are pigtail connections required or permissible?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Is pigtailing conductors at receptacles permissible or required?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are twist-type wire splices permitted under United States electrical code?" (asked by 3 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "I would through-wire with a single piece of wire, strip the conductor in the middle and wrap it around one device screw...I never knew if this met or violated any code. Any comments?" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:UgyvXJzwGdckjRnaBYR4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The reply states the termination method is code-compliant and does not alter NEC box fill calculations; it is commonly used to feed multiple devices in a multi-gang box.

Q: "Is this a joke? Electrical tape? 😂" (V:5o-TOjrwzus) (Q:Ugx5LdtgImGPWbvtS3Z4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Code or authority citation): Use a listed insulated splice connector inside a junction box; do not use electrical tape as a permanent splice method because it compromises conductor insulation and can cause overheating and fire. Follow NEC 110.14 for terminations and NEC 314 for box/enclosure requirements.

Q: "Is the anti-oxidant not required on the sub panel circuit breaker? I thought it was required for all aluminum connections." (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:Ugx3GGw76sJ0-jy4hvZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Code or authority citation): The responder indicates oxide inhibitor use is not mandatory for modern aluminum terminations, noting changes in aluminum alloys; however, Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) inspectors may still mandate its application.

Q: "I have 10ft of old wire but a 15ft run, how can I just join the pieces in the pipe with the twist on caps, or the push in connectors? Or do all connections of wire require another box? Can that box be covered with dry wall or does it have…" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:UgzrS0WJsvdh3nDrUxJ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): Splices must be made in an accessible junction box per NEC requirements; they cannot be concealed within raceway. The junction box may be installed flush with finished surfaces only if the cover remains removable and accessible, and box fill must be accounted for.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "Couldn’t 110.12(A) also apply to the argument from your last video about J-boxes and the need for there covers?" (V:qnYQg8dn0Dg) (Q:UgywNcTeZCBbNOxQySp4AaABAg)

family-q1-f04.chunkText:
# Licensing permits and code enforcement

A family of practitioner questions in the Permissibility and compliance type (Q1). These patterns concern authorization, qualifications, permits, inspections, jurisdictional rules, and compliance accountability.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 193 (10.2% of all Permissibility and compliance questions)
- Never received any reply: 113 (58.5%)
- Replied but unresolved: 18
- Answered: 62 (answer rate among the 80 replied questions: 77.5%)
- Question activity by year: 2018: 2, 2019: 13, 2020: 23, 2021: 29, 2022: 29, 2023: 36, 2024: 47, 2025: 14
- Main subject categories: Code Interpretation, Safety, and Field Operations (87), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (51), Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (31)

## Common question patterns
- "Which electrical tasks may homeowners legally perform on their own property?" (asked by 12 commenters)
- "Is it permissible for a homeowner to perform electrical wiring and hire an electrician only for final inspection?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Is formal schooling required to become or work as an electrician?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are electrical permits and inspections required for residential work?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Is removing an electrical utility meter or main service fuse permitted without authorization?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Can the property owner install the receptacle and lighting branch circuits themselves, subject to local requirements?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Is age a barrier to applying for an electrical apprenticeship?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Is a homeowner permitted to pull an electrical permit for self-performed work?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "I watched the whole video. It was amazing and inspiring. I have few questions, appologize me if I missed this information from the video: 1 - When building a VAN eletrical system Do I need to follow some sort of code and prepare for inspec…" (V:3Gr3rr4cPQQ) (Q:Ugz9KgCizsCApbSRXu14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report, Code or authority citation): The best reply recommends following each unit's manuals and established builder recommendations, notes no anti-fire treatment was used for the wooden enclosure, and estimates about $400 for necessary tools, highlighting a large crimper, coaxial cutters, and an adjustable wire stripper.

Q: "Can I just install myself the electrical (5 outlets and lighting)?" (V:fTODIqjuj7M) (Q:UgyKvWdzdUednGQNRy94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Verify local electrical code and permit/inspection requirements. Perform branch-circuit and subpanel rough-in where allowed, but have a licensed electrician complete the service feeder connection and approve the work for final inspection.

Q: "In Ontario, do you need to get inspected if you change a fixture or an outlet ?" (V:NfRuLlTp5s8) (Q:Ugy3D0jgLTNSmpZlJfx4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): The consensus answer: only a simple single-pole light switch replacement is commonly allowed without a permit; other work such as dimmers or outlets generally requires ESA/inspection.

Q: "Just out of curiosity, why the diazed fuses? I thought they were progressively phased out in Europe, is it a standard still very present in Germany? last time I saw this type of fuses, it was on a 30 year old machine, it was a pain to get…" (V:wsJONukJlLI) (Q:Ugwoq-C-NArw0XA5PpN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Use a certified safety relay (often dual‑channel or redundant contacts) for the emergency‑stop to prevent contact welding and ensure manual reset. Diazed/Neozed cartridges are still used as upstream main fuses for selectivity and to tolerate motor inrush currents.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "Are there building codes.? Is it a 10 page document?" (V:ruzEOYsZX-U) (Q:UgyJ2-x5QMGGfhLr8sJ4AaABAg)

# Cable support and physical protection

A family of practitioner questions in the Permissibility and compliance type (Q1). These patterns concern securing, supporting, routing, bending, and protecting cables through framing and other spaces.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 126 (6.7% of all Permissibility and compliance questions)
- Never received any reply: 75 (59.5%)
- Replied but unresolved: 10
- Answered: 41 (answer rate among the 51 replied questions: 80.4%)
- Question activity by year: 2013: 1, 2017: 1, 2019: 5, 2020: 16, 2021: 13, 2022: 22, 2023: 30, 2024: 25, 2025: 13
- Main subject categories: Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (74), Other/Unmapped (19), Code Interpretation, Safety, and Field Operations (15)

## Common question patterns
- "Are service loops permitted, and should excess conductor be trimmed?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "What code requirements apply to bundling current-carrying conductors?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Are listed electrical staples permitted for securing NM-B cable without damaging the conductors?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Are metal staples permitted for securing electrical cable in this installation?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Are protective plates or guards required or permitted to protect cables passing through framing?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Is a metal nailing plate required to protect conductors at stud penetrations?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are three NM cables permitted under one staple or cable connector?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are cable clamps permitted to secure multiple cables?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Stackers missing for 4 cables running down the 2x4 🧐" (V:PrJlFlL9I84) (Q:Ugy9VeakbI-YwEBLXBR4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Experience report): The practical solution offered is to staple the cables to the stud center rather than use stackers, keeping required edge clearance; local inspector interpretation may require nail plates or backing on exterior walls.

Q: "Just curious if you code allows a little extra loop for inside the wall at outlet and switch boxes? Just noticed everything seems tight." (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:UgyRj36wN9GTQztifSV4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Experience report): The selected reply asserts a 2020 code change permits a limited conductor loop (~6"). Other replies emphasize staple/clamp requirements and inspector discretion, so verify local enforcement.

Q: "Why staples doesn’t sound safe on electric wires" (V:l-gOTyql6RM) (Q:Ugw0HrD7DCsbeRkLTPZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): Staples listed for NM-B are permitted; use the correct staple type and avoid overdriving to prevent conductor insulation damage. Secure cables in accordance with NEC 334.30.

Q: "Are those wires exposed? No tubes? What do you do if one wire breaks? Like get drilled into or something?" (V:PrJlFlL9I84) (Q:UgyZrPUWoCDNuqNVpxp4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation, Prescription): The reply confirms conductors have insulation and outer sheathing, and warns that you must locate concealed conductors before drilling to avoid physical damage.

Q: "Is it not required to have that or some kind of grommet to protect against chafing? Second, dude throw on some safety glasses." (V:NfRuLlTp5s8) (Q:Ugzy0vrFmaboty9top94AaABAg)

family-q1-f06.chunkText:
# Branch circuit sizing and loading

A family of practitioner questions in the Permissibility and compliance type (Q1). These patterns concern circuit ratings, conductor ampacity, connected loads, overcurrent protection, and branch-circuit arrangements.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 121 (6.4% of all Permissibility and compliance questions)
- Never received any reply: 71 (58.7%)
- Replied but unresolved: 3
- Answered: 47 (answer rate among the 50 replied questions: 94.0%)
- Question activity by year: 2012: 1, 2018: 1, 2019: 11, 2020: 15, 2021: 21, 2022: 27, 2023: 20, 2024: 20, 2025: 5
- Main subject categories: Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (55), Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (23), Overcurrent, Short-Circuit, and Protective Devices (18)

## Common question patterns
- "Is it permissible to supply lighting and receptacles from the same branch circuit?" (asked by 9 commenters)
- "Is 14 AWG conductor permitted on a 15-ampere circuit?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are receptacle or circuit quantities limited on a branch circuit?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Are 14 AWG conductors permitted on a 20-ampere circuit?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Is a number 6 AWG conductor acceptable with a 70-ampere breaker?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Does a bathroom receptacle circuit require a minimum 20-ampere breaker and 12/2 cable?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Is an inline fuse required between a battery and its off switch or master isolator?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Is a neutral conductor required or permitted for a 240-volt circuit?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Thanks for the great video. Do you need a fuse between the battery and master switch?" (V:ycTi1SLmods) (Q:UgyqNEM3Vb9Y_0MEXNh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report, Code or authority citation): Install an inline main fuse on the battery positive feeder upstream of the master switch to protect the main conductor from overloads, while retaining individual branch circuit fusing; ensure placement complies with the cited ISO requirement near the battery.

Q: "the Electrical Code required to have 12/2 for bathroom for bathroom receptacle outlets and no other outlets" (V:NfRuLlTp5s8) (Q:UgxyvDGKHxfobRnxX6x4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Prescription, Code or authority citation): The reply advises Ontario/Canada allows 15 A/14-2 branch circuits; use one 14/2 GFCI-protected branch for bathroom receptacles and a separate 14/2 branch for lighting/fan.

Q: "Can I use a 30 amp breaker with 12 gauge wire ? Breaker going off when I plug in my outdoor electrical heater and I don’t have anymore room in my panel! Or would I have to run a sub panel?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgwAYF0N_mucQJWrzB54AaABAg)
A (Correction, Prescription, Code or authority citation): Recommends not upsizing the breaker; 12 AWG conductors are limited to 20 A per NEC 240.4(D). Use a properly sized 20 A branch circuit, reduce the heater load, or install a correctly wired subpanel to add circuits.

Q: "Can a 40 amp double pole breaker be used for a 30 amp breaker for a dryer?" (V:bGZVILwbyLo) (Q:UgwOBk3_ecrsu_97ryh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): The fix requires upgrading conductor ampacity and the receptacle to match the 40 A overcurrent device; otherwise using a 40 A breaker on a dryer circuit is noncompliant (see NEC 240.4 and NEC 310.15(B)(16)).

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "What if something happens to outlets circuit the light would cut out as will." (V:mEl294senUg) (Q:UgziW78rUHTIlKNIUcR4AaABAg)

family-q1-f07.title: Service equipment and panel configuration
family-q1-f07.chunkText:
# Service equipment and panel configuration

A family of practitioner questions in the Permissibility and compliance type (Q1). These patterns concern service equipment, meters, panels, disconnects, feeders, breakers, and service wiring arrangements.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 120 (6.3% of all Permissibility and compliance questions)
- Never received any reply: 63 (52.5%)
- Replied but unresolved: 9
- Answered: 48 (answer rate among the 57 replied questions: 84.2%)
- Question activity by year: 2019: 2, 2020: 15, 2021: 18, 2022: 28, 2023: 22, 2024: 24, 2025: 11
- Main subject categories: Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (81), Overcurrent, Short-Circuit, and Protective Devices (18), Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (8)

## Common question patterns
- "Can multiple GFCI receptacles be connected downstream using line or load terminals?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "Is the service meter or meter socket required to be located on the front or street-facing portion of the residence?" (asked by 7 commenters)
- "Does an exterior service disconnect make the interior panel a subpanel?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Is an unconnected circuit breaker permissible as a filler or spare in an open panel position?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Does code or the utility require the meter enclosure at the front center of the house?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Is it permissible for conductors feeding a panel to enter from the side or bottom?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Is manipulating, removing, or opening a utility meter or meter socket permitted?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Are service panels permitted inside a dwelling?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Can any size Amp breaker go in any open space in the electrical panel?" (V:bGZVILwbyLo) (Q:UgzYos2DHAc4HLUJhD54AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): Yes, conditionally: a breaker may occupy a panel slot provided its ampacity does not exceed the panelboard rating and the breaker type is listed for that panel (see NEC 110.3(B) and NEC overcurrent sizing rules).

Q: "Is it code for you to have the 220 panel on the outside? My main panel is located inside my garage, and only the meter box is on the outside. I would think this could greatly increase the air tightness having only a single wire/hole coming…" (V:xTpl7WYMkcA) (Q:Ugz2WLK8wuXrpOOctM14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): The practical solution is to provide an outdoor emergency disconnect (per NEC) while locating the main service panel indoors, which allows a single service-conductor penetration. The disconnect can often be mounted at or integrated with the meter base.

Q: "How can you have a 200 amp sub panel off a 200 amp main panel? Isn’t that a just second main panel?" (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:Ugw6q0kt9zTUSqG4byZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): A 200 A-rated subpanel is acceptable if the feeder conductor ampacity and overcurrent protection match the 200 A rating; this does not make it a separate service unless it has its own service disconnect. 200 A breakers and 4/0 AWG aluminum feeders are standard for this arrangement.

Q: "Better build a platform in front of that panel. Highest breaker can’t be more the 6ft 6 from the floor" (V:IZthjsIQ680) (Q:Ugyx_D_hQqi4vVH-25N4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation): A reply clarifies the intended maximum as 2 meters (6'7"). This provides a corrected measurement for determining whether a platform is required.

## Common question patterns
- "What conductor color-coding conventions apply to electrical wiring identification?" (asked by 10 commenters)
- "May white conductors used as ungrounded conductors be re-identified?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "May a neutral conductor be reidentified as an ungrounded conductor?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Is brown-orange-yellow conductor color coding a nationwide U.S. standard for 480-volt three-phase systems?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Can a blue or red conductor be used as a phase conductor?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is a blue-marked conductor permitted as a switched phase in Germany?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is a high-leg conductor required to be identified with orange under NEC 110.15?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Can a red-insulated conductor be used as the neutral conductor in a lighting circuit?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Black wire conned to white wire… isn’t there a mismatch of amp ratings/AWG there?" (V:Syn32MkFBg0) (Q:UgyXXibWhZsmbZ-WFzt4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Confirm the breaker overcurrent rating to determine conductor ampacity; a 15 A breaker requires 14 AWG conductors. Do not rely on sheath color for ampacity determination.

Q: "Sir s pagkabt po ng breaker OK b kht bliktad papntang ac," (V:gWLquD_xVIE) (Q:UgxSvAEUeKjB0-9sFwB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Explanation): The solution: for line-to-ground circuits interrupt the hot conductor at the switch and maintain protective earth continuity to the luminaire/appliance; do not route earth through the switch or leave hot permanently connected.

Q: "1. Don't you have to re identify the white 10 gage wire that you used for your water heater? To indicate it is not a neutral? 2. If you dig about a 12 inch hole and pour a tiny bit of water into it you and push down and work a ground rod i…" (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:UgxVBSIL7SOpZ6FLkhF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Re-identify the white 10 AWG conductor by marking it (e.g., black tape or paint) at both terminations. For 240 V appliances, use a 4‑wire cable with separate neutral and equipment grounding conductor.

Q: "I always thought that the red conductor in 14/3 wire was used as a traveler in 3-way switches. I guess I've been doing it wrong. :/" (V:LhZcWykPWQc) (Q:UgyHZ4o07ys3qqwwP0J4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Yes, red is commonly used as the traveler in 14/3 for 3‑way switching. The black conductor is usually the common (line or load); if only one cable is run, a white conductor used as an ungrounded conductor must be re‑identified (taped) accordingly.

## Common question patterns
- "Is GFCI protection required for bathroom, outdoor, garage, and similar receptacles?" (asked by 10 commenters)

- "Is GFCI protection required for the demonstrated installation?" (asked by 4 commenters)

- "Can additional receptacles be connected to the load terminals of a GFCI receptacle?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Does an outdoor 30-ampere RV receptacle require GFCI protection?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why do you need to install the GFCI?" (V:NyjtcnrLBNE) (Q:Ugz3vms1XYs5Cj05IfJ4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Correction): Responder asserts GFCI is required by code and specifies GFCI receptacle placement within 25 ft.

Q: "Does the GFCI circuit require a regular (non-GFCI) breaker? Also how many outlets can be on 15 Amp GFCI-protected circuit?" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:Ugwi1GitAZJkE7nW3rV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The reply confirms a GFCI breaker is not mandatory and that using multiple GFCI devices on one circuit can hinder fault isolation. It also notes the NEC has no fixed outlet-count limit and suggests eight outlets as a conservative practical maximum.

Q: "Does the daisy chain reduce the safety of using the GFCI?" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:UgwGk-Qbv__mGwJMC4R4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The reply confirms daisy-chaining from the GFCI does not reduce safety; when wired to the LOAD terminal, downstream receptacles receive ground-fault protection. Ensure correct line/load identification and secure terminations per NEC 210.8 and grounding requirements.

Q: "Should 30A RV outlet installed inside garage be GFCI protected, in which case I would need to install 30A GFCI breaker (don’t think I have ever seen 30A GFCI RV outlet)?" (V:4Xq8dddqxw8) (Q:UgxtlFiWBZlrQHE5VW94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Per the cited 2020 NEC (210.8), garage receptacles in dwelling units require GFCI protection. Verify device rating (30 A) and consult the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ).

A (Explanation, Code or authority citation, Prescription): The installer used NYM cables (NYM 3x1.5, NYM 5x1.5, NYM 5x2.5) and cites VDE EN 0298-4 / DIN 57100. He gives a rule-of-thumb ampacity of ~1 mm² per amp and notes 1.5 mm² is rated ~18 A in free air; enclosed routing requires derating.

Q: "Doesn’t the code state the neutral can not be disconnected at any given point on the Circuit when removing a device? So u must pigtail the neural" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:UgwhqPiozvD4djg8BMZ4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Correction, Explanation): The requirement applies to multi‑wire branch circuits with a shared neutral (see NEC 210.4); in those cases maintain neutral continuity and provide simultaneous disconnects. For single‑circuit neutrals, pigtailing is not mandated.

A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Hedged speculation): Use a stripper with a manufacturer-rated AWG range that includes 22 AWG stranded; a tool rated 12–22 AWG stranded should handle 22 AWG conductors and likely strip 22/4 and 22/2 jackets.

Q: "Can MC cable be used in residential or does it depend on local jurisdiction?" (V:Wk_mSDfaRTg) (Q:Ugw1fTY5KI8oGDAbxyx4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Reply indicates MC cable may be used in residential installations to provide conductor corrosion protection. Permissibility is dependent on the AHJ and local electrical code adoption.

A (Prescription, Explanation): Verify circuits are de-energized with a voltage tester, switch off power sources, and insulate or tape conductor ends to prevent shorts. Follow standard PPE and safe work procedures when servicing the system.

Q: "Do we need extra protection near the switches and outlets, where people touch things the most? Other thing, da fuq are those cork style fuses? What extra protection they give?" (V:wsJONukJlLI) (Q:Ugwg28xj6Coh7hstz094AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The practical recommendation is to use D-category MCBs or a soft starter to handle high inrush currents; cork screw fuses are antiquated and can create phase-loss hazards on three-phase loads.

Q: "is it really safe to walk away from the energized ground if needed?" (V:sBUvYh93pQc) (Q:UgjYuhTZSl-VXXgCoAEC)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Replies advise using a controlled shuffle to reduce step voltage and keeping feet together to maintain equipotential contact. Avoid falling to prevent creating a touch-voltage differential between hands and feet.

Q: "Excellent video Bob. Can you bend electrical PVC conduit with this tool?" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:Ugz-MJGavTAiELbunoR4AaABAg)

Q: "But how well does the universal wire strippers work for a COAXIAL cable (RG 6)?" (V:9hlo87E_GdQ) (Q:UgzSHHDSivZ78yRm36N4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction): Universal strippers can remove the RG-6 outer jacket but won't correctly trim the braid or strip the center-conductor insulation for connectorization. Use a dedicated coax stripper for jacket removal, braid trimming, and precise center-conductor preparation.

Q: "Is a basement considered a wet or damp location?" (V:OeuWsYy6bvE) (Q:UgzAwo07IB5iXhK9gVd4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): Classification depends on finishedness: an unfinished basement is at least a damp location while a finished basement is likely considered dry. Refer to NEC Article 100 'Location' definitions for formal criteria.

Q: "Is a basement considered wet location?" (V:OeuWsYy6bvE) (Q:Ugz32-mRMsX0CX9MyQt4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Basements that are normally dry are not classified as wet locations under NEC Article 100. Regardless, receptacles in basements require GFCI protection per NEC 210.8.

Q: "Is IP-rating not a thing in the USA?" (V:LdNuJksviTY) (Q:UgyRJ9bkMzzDuLDtvC94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): IP enclosure ratings are used, primarily for outdoor enclosures; solid-object ingress protection (IP2X/IP4X) is important for safety even indoors.

Q: "Sink water obviously doesn’t count with the 36” water contact rule for switches ?" (V:NfRuLlTp5s8) (Q:UgzSLNxFt_KhTGncVl54AaABAg)
A (Correction, Prescription): The responder advises that sink water does count and that switches/receptacles within the 36-inch zone should be protected by a GFCI device.

Q: "Can i connect the inverter to the load output of the controller?" (V:HQ4SfbeGg5s) (Q:UgzlXuMQDO11gvXmZuN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Explanation): The reply advises against connecting the inverter to the controller load output because MPPT load terminals lack sufficient current capacity; connect the inverter to the battery with appropriate protection.

Q: "Sir can't some one use only the panel controller and battery only?" (V:HQ4SfbeGg5s) (Q:UgxwMQRq7qFkhWA4opF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Yes, a PV array connected to a charge controller and battery will charge the battery without loads connected. Connecting loads to the controller provides telemetry and load-management benefits and helps identify parasitic draws.

Q: "i have two batteries conected 12V system. can i connect main motor and accessories if so do i just connect main motor as usual?" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:UgwGiEUjXUkcBfYFaM94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Parallel battery connection maintains system voltage at 12 V; connect the motor positive through appropriately sized conductors and overcurrent protection. Tie all negative returns to the battery negative bus and avoid hull bonding.

Q: "Great video! If I’m not charging off my alternator, do I need the BMS device?" (V:mRU80jmO7lA) (Q:UgzBicXcj6QhIeGbgU94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): A BMS is required to manage and protect LiFePO4 cells even if alternator charging is not present. Victron implements an external BMS for protection and system control.

Q: "Whats the reason they dont want round boxes used when locknuts are required?" (V:JnkK_yVQkaU) (Q:UgzUP_MSAbBgflN1sJB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Round/pancake boxes generally have no side knockouts to accept threaded conduit connectors with locknuts or bushings, so they cannot be used for side conduit terminations. Use boxes with side knockouts or top-entry conduit per NEC Article 314.

Q: "How do you connect all those wires to a single terminal in a circuit breaker? I know the typical legal solution is to use dual-wire lugs in a single breaker. But is legal to use two breakers in parallel, each rated 250 A?" (V:BfYHDkMAINM) (Q:UgxG3aVZgxB-auaMX6Z4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Code or authority citation): Use a single overcurrent device or service equipment that has manufacturer-listed multi-conductor lugs per phase to terminate parallel conductors. Do not parallel two separate breakers; terminations must follow the breaker/terminal listing and NEC terminal requirements.

Q: "as an electrical apprentice i have a question about the code, can you put more than 4 wires through a hole ?" (V:dpyvYfU2JLk) (Q:UgwHCEyA15M8N-1jjSV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Hedged speculation): Practical guidance: provide sufficient penetration diameter and avoid tightly grouped conductors in insulated cavities to preserve cooling. AHJ interpretations differ, so limiting to two conductors per hole reduces thermal issues and inspection risk.

Q: "but going more then 360 turns isn't to code, is it, or is it that you are not pulling thru more then 360 at a time the reason for the code so that you don't stress the wire with resistance? The radius seems ok because its individual wires…" (V:SsdC6nZXhdg) (Q:UgxQfO2_wfcq5-n61ex4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The 360° limitation refers to the maximum cumulative bend between pull points; additional total turns are acceptable if intermediate pull points (junctions/LBs) keep each pull ≤360°.

Q: "The hotspot manufacturer is calling for a number 8 AWG copper with a 2 pole 50 amp circuit breaker GFCI. It's in there diagram and schematics showing all number 8's. I wanted to run number 6 gauge copper but their terminals would not fit i…" (V:mTlqGS81B-k) (Q:UgxKfAp3tr7G55S1rEh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The available solution indicates #8 AWG copper is acceptable if its ampacity meets 50 A based on conductor insulation and temperature rating per NEC tables. Do not force improper lug fit, use the specified conductor size, correct terminals, or a manufacturer-approved connector.

Q: "So in a wet damp location what do you run in conduit." (V:OeuWsYy6bvE) (Q:UgyNcgspFXvyxZ3r5j54AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Use conductors with a 'W' wet-location insulation rating (e.g., THW, MTW) or UF cable for conduit in wet/damp locations. Verify compliance with conduit fill and derating requirements per NEC.

Q: "Shouldn’t 4AWG be used with a 70A breaker according to the NEC?" (V:SsdC6nZXhdg) (Q:UgwBDin7oRAsXwWxMGF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): Primary responder asserts 6 AWG THWN in conduit meets NEC ampacity for a 70 A OCPD using the 75°C column; NM-B wiring would require 4 AWG. Secondary replies advise considering #4 for voltage-drop/continuous-load scenarios and call out exterior disconnect, grounding/bonding, and conductor identification requirements.

Q: "What number , group wire you used for 100 amp panel" (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:UgwGYwKSxMyrTOZmSxF4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Referral): The primary responder cites NEC Table 250.66 and Table 310.16, implying #6 AWG copper for the grounding conductor and referencing ampacity/terminal temperature requirements for the 100 A installation; verify with the AHJ.

Q: "Overall, these look like pretty decent machines for the money. What kind of run time can you get on a full charge, and what kind of batteries are they using?😉" (V:WLOQhEmmYw8) (Q:UgxSnYLNPhED78mSJEd4AaABAg)

A (Explanation, Correction): The two 270 Ah 12 V cells wired in series yield a 24 V, 270 Ah bank equal to 6.804 kWh of stored energy; available power depends on inverter continuous/peak ratings, not just kWh.

Q: "Ok having watched this many many times some ??'s still persist. 1. So home hook ups are NOT multiple phase? I always thought that special dryer plug meant more than one phase. 2. So when you hook up a house, what determines the amp service…" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:UgxRkDLTN_a6eKrudlB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Residential power is single‑phase split‑phase (two hot legs). Service ampacity is set by the distribution panel/main breaker per ampacity and local code; add a feeder or separate meter/panel for significant outbuilding loads.

Q: "How many amps in total will that be if there are 3 pairs of conductors and there are 3 1,200 amp fuses??" (V:BfYHDkMAINM) (Q:UgwbyCLeZEw_TR-p5FJ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Explanation): Each feeder set is protected at 1,200 A, so per-phase current is 1,200 A. Do not sum phase currents for a three-phase rating; each parallel feeder set must be sized for 1,200 A.

Q: "I’d like to know your electric costs. And how many amps is your main board? I’m wanting to do 40 spots and I think I’ll need a 2,000 amp board" (V:EP2inIH0xXs) (Q:Ugyv2t29uAm7ajzOBTF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): A reply applied diversity/demand factors (CEC Table 71) to reduce aggregate load and reported a calculated service requirement of 1,440 A for 40 fifty-amp pedestals.

Q: "What is the total connected load to be assumed in calculation for the building?" (V:098UloW6xfk) (Q:Ugy2zHcLLQHwSjmVkNB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The practical solution is either to use transformer capacity as the design constraint (apply a loading factor, as illustrated) or to sum all connected loads and then size the transformer accordingly.

## Example questions and answers
Q: "What is maximum number of lights and outlets in one electric line. I want to put up lots of lights and outlets in my new garage ... the limit that max I don’t know." (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:Ugzg0aR_ZQdKT83a8F54AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Referral): The reply claims a code limit of 10 outlets per branch circuit and directs the asker to a video explaining a sizing formula for lights and outlets per circuit.

Q: "The hot water tank don't need 10/3 cable? If both black and white is hot?" (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:UgxNm5KfdHgAI6E7ixd4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Use 10/2 with ground for a dedicated 240 V water-heater branch circuit. The white conductor may be used as an ungrounded conductor if properly re-identified per NEC re-identification rules.

Q: "Thx for all the great videos. I’m working on wiring my house and your videos are extremely informative and helpful. Is there a rule of thumb or formula on how long a home run should be? I’m working with 12 and 14 gauge. Thx a million" (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:UgzaF-PTgZiiVNR8thF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Practical solution: increase conductor size for runs ~80 ft+ to mitigate voltage drop and heating. The voltage-drop formula is the formal method for exact sizing; using larger wire is conservative.

Q: "How do you know which wire hooks up to which fuse. Like 5 amp 10amp 15 amp so on. Light lights go to which amp fuse and bilge pump so on" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:UgyRgF34EvBQ1YFjk3F4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Calculate circuit current from load wattage (account for motor inrush), choose conductor ampacity above the expected current, and select a fuse rated at or below the conductor ampacity but above normal load current.

Q: "Sweet, Question? How many outlets would be safe to run with one 20 Amp Breaker?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgwKM9xuHGgpWrwI4ZN4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Explanation): Apply the NEC 220 3 VA/ft2 load calculation to size general-use branch circuits; there is no fixed receptacle count. Ensure continuous loads remain <=80% of the 20 A breaker (16 A) and use 12 AWG conductors sized to breaker ampacity.

Q: "does it matter how many outlets you put on 1 line??" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgwpYze5I4turLrHjbl4AaABAg)

Q: "Is there a specific amp fuse I should be using or could I get away with all 10s or whatever? I bought a boat used that is pre wired but just missing fuses. Wondering if I have to look up the bilge, and LEDs and find the specific fuse they…" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:UgxPZu1aQqhvF37Vm594AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Select fuses to protect the wiring: compute max load current (I = P/V), pick conductor ampacity higher than the load, then use a fuse rated ≤ conductor ampacity but > load current. Note appliance plug fuses protect the device; extension-lead fuses protect the extension cable.

Q: "wiring stuff isnt hard, the problem comes to know when to use the right fuses etc. thinking about rewiring our boat, but the issue with what to fuse off etc still persist. i know its basics. you got a battery, that connects to the ignition…" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:Ugzwtp1WHlf99xsU2Vd4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report): Recommend determining each accessory's maximum current draw and selecting the next higher standard fuse rating (e.g., 3.7 A -> 5 A fuse). This is presented as a practical fuse‑sizing heuristic.

Q: "If I run two 360 GPH bilge pumps, each needing a 2.5 amp fuse, to one lead heading back to my fuse box and rocker switch (total length to the battery and back is ~15 ft), what size fuse should I use on the box? Do I add the draw together a…" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:UgxHNIvnbrDJooMQOxJ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription): The reply advises selecting a 12 A or 15 A fuse for the shared bilge pump circuit as a practical recommendation.

Q: "Anyone know how many watts most LED nav lights are? Trying to size my fuse but no mention on the packaging" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:Ugx-5sL_uj7DCxIIpRl4AaABAg)
A (Prescription): Reply provides a practical overcurrent-protection recommendation: assume <2 A steady-state and install a 5 A fuse. Verify with manufacturer ratings and account for conductor ampacity and any inrush.

Q: "how far a way from the wall is the smoke detector, in bed room and living room. and what is the height of the meter box [ one meter or forty meters heights] . your video are very informative." (V:TElw-O8ps4I) (Q:Ugz1twtgmT0SJKL_vFh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Referral): Meter-box height is determined by the local utility; the electrical code does not set panel mounting height. NEC/CEC 240.24 sets a maximum breaker-handle centerline of 6 ft‑7 in; smoke alarms have no specific horizontal wall distance in the code but require 3 ft clearance from HVAC registers and fan blades, verify with the local authority having jurisdiction.

Q: "Min. 14' long pole: is that above ground? How deep in the ground must it be placed?" (V:gJ75hYJYLb8) (Q:Ugzorbd4kVR5Kt8UvCN4AaABAg)

Q: "A questions that I have always had: How many holes can be drilled through studs and joists before they compromise the integrity of the structure? Does spacing matter?" (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:UgyWyzwlEjURFGCeUU14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): The best reply provides numeric hole-diameter limits: 40% of stud width for load-bearing/exterior walls and 60% for interior non-load-bearing. It also recommends verifying local code and manufacturer specifications for exceptions.

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why do you clip the cables within the walls. How do you clip cables after the wall sheets are installed." (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:UgycW71VJCehvGEPTMZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): The practical solution given is that nonmetallic-sheathed cable (NMSC) must be mechanically secured at regular intervals (every ~4 ft) and within 12 inches of each junction or device box to provide support and strain relief at panel and box entries.

Q: "Can I ask how you ran power to the shed? Perhaps there is another video I have not seen? If not, I have to connect to the main panel in the cabin and run underground, most likely through a conduit at at least 12inches down. Any suggestions?" (V:fTODIqjuj7M) (Q:Ugx3FuqGEzoBCoy-qdt4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): The solution: an underground feeder was run from a junction box on the main service to a 50 A subpanel in the shop. Follow local burial-depth requirements and install warning tape over the buried conductor.

Q: "how did you nail the box to the joist if there's drywall up around the box cutout? Why would there be a dry walled over box already in the wall and not wired when the wall was open? I'm lost on this question, Do you just knock out a bigger…" (V:7xFsDCzb6Sg) (Q:Ugzxu6VFAAjtZDPcFl94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Use an old-work (cut-in) electrical box for retrofits; new-work boxes are secured to studs prior to drywall. Old-work boxes clamp to the drywall, avoiding the need to nail to the joist.

Q: "Ok how in the hell do you run a new line through an attic to an air-conditioner the line has to come out of an eve theres no way to transition from romex to single strand without one touching the wrong area." (V:OeuWsYy6bvE) (Q:UgxOFR-PoZp1SqZwCWd4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Recommend installing an accessible junction box in the attic and perform an NM-to-THHN transition, or use UF cable for the run, to meet NEC splice accessibility and conductor type requirements.

## Common question patterns

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Can you tell me how to add 240V to 120 central Pannel? Thanks!" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:Ugy7yMP7QHPEQjESBGV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): You must have split-phase service with two 120 V hot legs 180° out of phase to get 240 V; this requires the proper utility/transformer configuration or a service upgrade and installation of a two-pole breaker per NEC by a licensed electrician.

Q: "Great video. So now that the panel is grounded how do you switch out old two wire outlets to grounded 3 wire ones?" (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:UgxkGijWC2jnhZFBOil4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): The primary solution is to install a continuous equipment grounding conductor back to the service grounding/bonding system or bond to an approved metallic water‑service conductor. Where an EGC cannot be run, replacing the receptacle with a GFCI and marking 'No Equipment Ground' is an NEC‑permitted alternative (see NEC 406.4(D)(2)).

Q: "So if you wanted to add a receptacle after the gfci would you connect your hot and neutral out of the line side to the next gfci outlet? I'm confused on when you would connect out of the load side of the receptacle." (V:GixfggjsqCY) (Q:Ugyq4sFe6Jv9CCmTL0t4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Solution: use a GFCI breaker for the whole circuit or install the GFCI receptacle first and use its load terminals to feed downstream devices; alternatively provide a dedicated neutral conductor to avoid imbalance tripping.

Q: "Hey when Dad plugs into that 30amp outlet with the adapter. Please figure out how to add a GFCI into that conversion. You don't need that for the RV, but dear old Dad will be using a hand held drill or pruner, etc..." (V:yiV8YYgakPo) (Q:Ugw9La0rxMCrJNKheQ14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction): The recommended fix is a portable GFCI pigtail used with a 30 A-to-15 A adapter to provide ground-fault protection. Ensure conductor ampacity and overcurrent protection are coordinated, do not rely on GFCI for overload protection and avoid using smaller-gauge extension cords on a 30 A circuit.

## At a glance

## Common question patterns

## Example questions and answers
Q: "i watched about 9 or 10 generac videos yours was the most explanatory, i was confused about when your supposed to pull the N1 and N2 fuses to keep them from blowing." (V:_IDluE3fEoc) (Q:Ugzd59iKiLc5RuXaSCN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report, Correction): Removing N1/N2 fuses is optional; installers often remove them to protect against accidental shorting during wiring. For the generator feed the installer specified 2-2-4-6 Al quad for a 100 A generator, and the generator output (100 A) governs feeder ampacity, not the house 200 A service.

Q: "Can we convert 1phase to 3 phase voltage?" (V:qthuFLNSrlg) (Q:Ugxydo5JGJRl0Au2EbF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): A motor-generator or rotary phase converter driven by single-phase can produce three-phase output; it's a feasible solution but less efficient than native three-phase service or a proper three-phase transformer.

Q: "can you explain better why we need to remove the fuses? and when do we put it back?" (V:_IDluE3fEoc) (Q:Ugzuqr26-Wav0TCBzPJ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Remove the transfer switch fuses during installation to prevent nuisance fuse operation from wiring surges or accidental faults. Reinstall the fuses after all conductors and connections are complete and before initial energization.

Q: "How did you hook up to the alternator charging? Did you use the CCP? If so, how did you get the 80 amp output down to 60 amps?" (V:s5d826UHNw8) (Q:UgzDNFUjaBlWrcdVqm14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The alternator feed was connected at the jumper cable connection terminal; the EcoFlow's input/charge acceptance limits the charging current to 60 A, so the alternator's 80 A capability is not imposed on the circuit.

## Common question patterns

- "How should the grounding electrode system be installed and connected?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How can an earth or ground-rod installation be tested for low resistance?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "How are equipment grounding conductors terminated in receptacle boxes?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "How can a grounded receptacle be installed when conductors measure about 208 volts to neutral?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "How can a grounding bypass be understood and mitigated when protecting the grounding path?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "How can a grounding electrode be installed without a ladder, and which rod material is suitable?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "How can a grounding electrode or ground rod be located on a property?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "what do you do with the load ground line to the next outlet? Are you running a pigtail to the single GFCI ground connection?" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:UgzAMCxv1__djpkuIw94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Install a pigtail (bonding jumper) from the incoming and outgoing equipment grounding conductors to the GFCI grounding screw so the EGC remains continuous. This preserves downstream grounding continuity per NEC 250.148.

Q: "How do we connect the earth in scenario where the meter is on the utility pole" (V:lH1pchxXFFs) (Q:UgxyOCEuIPPFryC2dqN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Install a grounding electrode conductor (GEC) from the consumer unit earth/grounding terminal to an earth electrode (rod) and make a secure bond per NEC 250. Verify GEC sizing, clamps, and bonding practices comply with local code; do not rely on utility pole metalwork as the customer earth.

Q: "Where does the bare wire go?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgzTh0-uhT-sAT9IMSh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): The bare conductor is the equipment grounding conductor and is terminated on the grounding bus/bar in the service or distribution panel. In subpanels, maintain neutral/ground separation per NEC.

Q: "I’m confused about the ponytailed grounds. How can we tie 2 ground together and connect both connected ground to the ground screw on the outlet????" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgwhThBZrRNRX8S_NYF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Splice the equipment grounding conductors together and attach a pigtail to the receptacle grounding screw, or use a listed green connector with a hole to extend one conductor. This practice satisfies NEC 250.148 for grounding conductor splices and device grounding.

A (Prescription, Correction, Explanation): The recommended action is to either remain stationary or perform the controlled shuffle with feet together. Hopping risks falling and creating a larger distance between contact points, increasing lethal step potential.

Q: "They just told us at a safety responders training to hop not shuffle lol which is it." (V:sBUvYh93pQc) (Q:UgjRzwAHAl6_GHgCoAEC)

Q: "what if u run off?" (V:sBUvYh93pQc) (Q:UgzdLyKbgH0ljvjdO6p4AaABAg)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "how can i charge my battery without solar panels" (V:HQ4SfbeGg5s) (Q:UgwekKGRbB-AczKJcq14AaABAg)
A (Prescription): Use a dedicated mains battery charger matched to the battery voltage and chemistry; ensure proper polarity, overcurrent protection (MCB/fuse), and earthing/grounding when connecting to AC mains.

Q: "How would I wire up a starter battery to my outboard and have 2 leisure batteries. Using a dc/dc charger please?" (V:ycTi1SLmods) (Q:UgzcjWmP5n4GrDyEJcR4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Creator meta-response): Measure the starter motor's cranking current and compare to leisure battery discharge capability. If leisure batteries lack required cranking current, install a dedicated starting battery and provide dedicated charging (separate charger or appropriately configured DC-DC charger).

Q: "What if you have 24v solar panels for your van?" (V:mRU80jmO7lA) (Q:UgzeGjussCtf_VSGOk94AaABAg)
A (Prescription): The recommended solution is to use a solar charge controller or inverter/charger that accepts the 24 V PV input and regulates charging to the battery bank per the battery charging profile. Ensure the controller/inverter's PV input voltage range and MPPT capability match the 24 V array and the battery system voltage.

Q: "So what happens if it runs out of battery while you're working in the field? Do you have to bring out a generator to charge it or do you have to bring out a trailer and haul it out with the truck" (V:WLOQhEmmYw8) (Q:Ugy1mF2yIMRgIagWqV14AaABAg)
A (Prescription): Recommend using a portable battery generator/inverter for field charging and monitoring the state-of-charge via the loader's gauge to avoid being stranded.

# Grounding Bonding and Fault Paths

A family of practitioner questions in the Conceptual type (Q4). These patterns address grounding conductors, bonding, neutral connections, grounding electrodes, and fault-current return paths.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 275 (12.9% of all Conceptual questions)

- Answered: 117 (answer rate among the 171 replied questions: 68.4%)
- Question activity by year: 2014: 2, 2018: 1, 2019: 24, 2020: 32, 2021: 63, 2022: 43, 2023: 34, 2024: 52, 2025: 24
- Main subject categories: Grounding, Bonding, and Fault Management (139), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (71), Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (29)

## Common question patterns
- "How are neutral and equipment grounding conductors bonded at service equipment and separated downstream?" (asked by 37 commenters)
- "Why is a grounding conductor connected to building metalwork or equipment?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "What is the purpose of grounding and earthing in an electrical installation?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "What are the relationships among the neutral, grounding, and return conductors?" (asked by 7 commenters)
- "How does an equipment grounding conductor differ from a neutral conductor?" (asked by 7 commenters)
- "How do grounding and lightning-protection paths relate?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why does current return to its source through a return path?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why does a neutral conductor carry return current?" (asked by 6 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why do you use two electrodes" (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:UgyJPbHNByw2Nx_q0z54AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation, Prescription): The accepted solution per replies references the NEC threshold: a single rod is permitted only if the ground-rod resistance is under 25 Ω, which is rarely achievable in practice, so two rods are usually installed to meet grounding electrode system requirements.

Q: "Why is it some builders use switches and outlets with no ground wire screw in new construction? My home, built in the 80s is this way and I have to pigtail a ground wire connection whenever I replace a switch or outlet." (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:Ugx58RJgYRr61CiAUXh4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation, Prescription): Conduit and metal boxes can serve as the equipment grounding conductor under NEC 250.118(4). Adding a pigtail to the device is optional but commonly done for device grounding assurance and UL compliance.

Q: "very neat, thank you, it's nice when you know what your doing and have the right tools, live in a mobile home and just want to ground my antenna, have one question, why 2 grounding rods." (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:UgylzTAhMCB_eU4xxXB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The recommended solution is to install a supplementary grounding electrode to achieve a lower ground electrode resistance and comply with the cited NEC provision. Two rods are used to meet the <25 Ω resistance target and code requirements.

Q: "can u splain simple words why the neutral and ground are conected togheter?" (V:ZQOTvsXtrKo) (Q:UgyOH18wrLVunITjW0d4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation, Prescription): Per NEC 250, the neutral (grounded conductor) is bonded to the equipment grounding conductor and grounding electrode at the service disconnect; interior sub-panels require the neutral bus to be isolated from the ground bus.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "How curious. Here in Brazil I was told to never connect the ground rod to the neutral wire, as it would be a bad and unsafe pratice. Never got a decent explanation, but yours make sense." (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:Ugz6iu7juGmp-W0Onal4AaABAg)

Q: "5:18 can we touch neutral wire safely when AC/DC current is flowing? if so, then how is it safe to touch the bulb body when it is connected to the same neutral bus bar?" (V:UBERduCp3Wo) (Q:UgzfmtcYPo0VQhkNJ-B4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): The responder advises not to touch the neutral conductor since it carries return current and can form a body-to-earth fault path. The equipment grounding conductor can carry leakage current and thus may also be unsafe.

Q: "Why does he show power coming from the - neg pole of the battery and to the + pos pole. Should be the other way around unless I am missing something. Also the +pos wire should be red and the - neg wire should be black when dealing with DC…" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:Ugykhfn7LLMS5w4Acjx4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Correction, Referral): The reply states actual electron flow direction is from negative to positive in DC, whereas conventional current notation defines current opposite to electron flow. A supplemental video link on battery operation was provided.

Q: "Great video but the flow off dc power supply starts from the + not - side of a battery doesn’t it ??? This is throwing me off. Please correct me if I’m wrong." (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:UgwRUMM1an5e7dsQOM94AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Correction, Referral): The respondent clarifies that actual electron flow is from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. They note the pedagogical convention of using conventional current (positive-to-negative) for circuit analysis.

Q: "Why is it that when I connect 2 lamps in series they give out light but when I connect 3 or more they don't give out light." (V:lH1pchxXFFs) (Q:Ugx8t5tm6plwG1wRY9B4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Prescription): The replies correctly identify voltage division across series-connected lamp filament resistances as the cause; connecting each lamp in parallel provides full supply voltage to every lamp.

# Branch Circuits and Lighting Controls

A family of practitioner questions in the Conceptual type (Q4). These patterns explain branch-circuit arrangements, switches, lighting, receptacles, travelers, and fixture wiring.

- Main subject categories: Devices, Lighting, and Utilization Equipment (62), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (18), Grounding, Bonding, and Fault Management (6)

## Common question patterns
- "Why do switches have particular terminal or mounting arrangements?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "How are line and load conductors arranged when a receptacle is controlled by a switch?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How are multiple three-way switches and a luminaire interconnected?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why are neutral conductors not normally switched?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why does a ceiling fan require protective earthing?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How does a switch control a luminaire?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How can a failed receptacle interrupt downstream receptacles?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are standard receptacles rated as they are?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Hooking up the outlets like you do, not pigtailing but just putting the wires on the other screws if the first outlet goes bad does that stop power to the next one?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgyWCY-03rpYdWD-VRN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Yes, a non-pigtailed receptacle serving as feed-through creates a single-point failure; device loss opens the branch circuit. Use pigtail connections sized to conductor ampacity and rated device terminals to preserve continuity.

Q: "To be clear, is this an example of wiring a circuit in a series? I've read that it's better to run home circuits in parallel. What am I missing or misunderstanding?" (V:1D5OqJ5SF_I) (Q:UgySEz8rfHEIc8nEYut4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation, Prescription): Clarifies the circuit is a parallel branch circuit. Recommends making a joint and using pigtails or separate junctions to keep each receptacle independent instead of relying on device terminals.

Q: "What's the reason for code to require a neutral wire if it's not connected?" (V:jhwmBYgdcf4) (Q:UgwoAGbEF5sJVDteoVN4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): The neutral conductor is not required for the operation of a simple single-pole switch, but modern code requires a grounded conductor at the switch location to support future electronic control devices. NEC provisions (grounded conductor at switch locations) ensure dimmers, timers, and smart switches that need a neutral can be installed without rewiring.

Q: "Who installs electrical outlets upside down?" (V:jPC4hiVe_3w) (Q:UgwS_DBWRYE_mhJYP_p4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Correction): The OP cites code: NEC/NFPA contain no requirement for receptacle orientation, so both orientations comply with code.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "Is that outlet circuit part of the bathroom circuit?" (V:Jpu-3zB8Pqs) (Q:UgxYRlAahKefCFD-TWd4AaABAg)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Honest question…Why isn’t residential wiring done in conduit?" (V:PrJlFlL9I84) (Q:UgyArgjvYRO9S5fazZh4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Experience report, Code or authority citation): Respondents note conduit is avoided primarily for cost reasons and because the NEC permits nonmetallic-sheathed cable in concealed, low-risk locations (see NEC 334.10 and 334.12).

Q: "Well done video. Curious about one thing; are the blocks attached to the roof?" (V:67I387enHcU) (Q:Ugzw-C7apv4X7lEjsj14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Confirms the conduit support blocks are non-penetrating ballasted supports and are not mechanically fastened to the roof; no roof screws are required.

Q: "Anybody know the reason why that it's mandatory to use emt. Cause I've never heard of a situation of when you would need this?" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:UgyO9IuiqqM-zA6XzBp4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): The reply asserts a fire-protection justification: EMT preserves circuit routing and conductor support during fire, unlike NM cable. This aligns with fire-code-driven requirements for raceways in some installations.

Q: "Other than because the code says so, what is the issue with, for example, running Romex in a conduit, under concrete, to a kitchen island?" (V:OeuWsYy6bvE) (Q:UgxPhybmotWVBE8r3JR4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): The reply identifies moisture-induced insulation degradation of NM as the core problem, implying underground conduit is a wet location per NEC 300.5 and thus unsuitable for Romex.

# Electrical Safety Hazards

A family of practitioner questions in the Conceptual type (Q4). These patterns concern shock, arcing, energized equipment, lightning, and other electrical dangers.

## At a glance

- Main subject categories: Grounding, Bonding, and Fault Management (34), Overcurrent, Short-Circuit, and Protective Devices (17), Code Interpretation, Safety, and Field Operations (15)

## Common question patterns
- "Why does an electrical shock occur under these conditions?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "Why does touching a neutral bus usually cause no sensation?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "How do step and touch voltage hazards occur around energized equipment?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why does a direct hot-to-neutral connection create a short circuit?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "What happens when resistance or a poor connection causes conductors to heat?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why do electrical faults, shocks, or protective devices behave this way?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How does the short-step technique reduce step-potential shock?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why might a hot-to-ground fault fail to trip an overcurrent device?" (asked by 3 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why do you wear gloves? I’m assuming it isn’t a live cable?" (V:HC2LPGocvFE) (Q:Ugx6s3i3FqnNZXIKMAN4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Prescription, Explanation): The gloves shown provide mechanical/cold protection, not electrical insulation. Energized work requires rated rubber insulating gloves with leather protectors under approved live-line permits; otherwise de-energize and use lockout/tagout.

Q: "why do they say neutral is safe.. its not it is still 120v." (V:UBERduCp3Wo) (Q:Ugxs4ggzgkP8TqCQzq54AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation, Prescription): The practical guidance: neutral may be at ground potential when the circuit is open, but when the circuit is closed it carries return current and can be live, so treat neutral as potentially energized and avoid contact or de-energize before touching.

Q: "what if the neutral wire touch the casing? Circuit breaker will not trip and you can still be electrocuted if you touch the casing, correct? In reality you have the Neutral bar connect to earth which will make it 0V but in your example the…" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:UgxOv_F_GG5i_H7GUnV4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Correction, Prescription): The best reply emphasizes that neutral is normally near earth potential due to bonding, but an open neutral or absent equipment grounding conductor can produce an energized-casing fault; verify with instruments.

Q: "I’ve been an electrician for a long time and I’ll be honest I still don’t understand why most of the time you can’t get shocked in a neutral but sometimes you can. Anyone wanna help me understand ?" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:UgxafJ5sni0aTTcjRIB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Measure neutral-to-ground voltage at the service/panel to detect a floating or improperly bonded neutral. If voltage is present, restore the bonding jumper (transformer/service bonding screw) and retest.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "How to get a fire if your casing wears down" (V:RtLg2sW0CY0) (Q:UgzLfk9W60vLRwZv4A54AaABAg)

## Common question patterns

- "How do 220/240-volt appliance circuits operate?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How do three-phase conductors relate in phase and waveform?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How do three-phase line-to-line voltages relate to phase voltages?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How do three-phase systems differ from single-phase systems?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How does the high leg of a delta system relate to its voltage relative to neutral or ground?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "What are the differences among phase, line, neutral, and earth conductors?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are three phases used instead of four or more?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "5 minutes in you say that no current need flow back thru the neutral if the current draw on both legs balance. I'm questioning that." (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:Ugx7mkZJmOQM_GDoR-14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The practical solution is to measure conductor currents with a clamp‑on ammeter; a perfectly balanced split‑phase load yields near‑zero neutral current, but imbalances and ground/earth paths can produce residual currents.

Q: "So in other words. Domestic homes in US and Canada doesn't have 3-phase appliance like we do in Europe? Most houses and newer apartments in Denmark have 4 wires going in with three phases and a neutral fed from a delta/wye transformer. Can…" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:Ugw6EhhmlMRWPs-JUUh4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Experience report, Referral): The best reply explains US homes use single-phase split-phase 120/240 V with two hot legs and a neutral, sometimes a separate equipment grounding conductor (four-wire service). Three-phase is generally reserved for industrial/commercial loads or large residences.

Q: "the orange that represents 208 is in a 120-D 3 phase system. a 120-Y system doesnt provide 240v only 120-208... the 120-D has 120 phase to neutral and 240v phase to phase except the orange wich is called the high leg. is that phase to neut…" (V:LhZcWykPWQc) (Q:UgzzJHXGoq6h3HD1zVF4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Prescription): The high leg on a 4‑wire delta (120/240) is approximately 208 V to neutral; ensure correct phase identification to avoid placing single‑pole breakers on the high leg and causing equipment failure.

Q: "what is the importance of 208V? What do you do with it? How do you reduce its power?" (V:LhZcWykPWQc) (Q:Ugzkuqr2IXt9jXuXDSp4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The 208 V high leg is intended to be paired with another phase for 240 V two- or three-pole loads rather than used by itself. Use multi‑pole breakers or a transformer/VFD to change voltage or control delivered power.

Q: "But are you not changing the resistance of the wire when you cut it in half" (V:VHNRHKVVClw) (Q:UgzYksvCDn9O_aHEqFJ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): The temporary pull splice is removed after installation and fresh conductor ends are used for final termination, so circuit resistance is not permanently changed. Do not cut strands off because that reduces conductor cross-section and impairs lug seating/termination.

Q: "I know virtually nothing about wiring. Is the sub-panel fed from the main panel?" (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:UgzVJSxdMmN3Ie_a73h4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The feeder conductors are routed through feed-through lugs on the main panel; the main service breaker provides overcurrent protection. The subpanel is main-lug-only and lacks a local main breaker.

Q: "Just out curiosity for my learning mind, what undesired effect would you had faced if you drilled directly above the switch box for fishing your wire instead of drilling off to the side?" (V:7xFsDCzb6Sg) (Q:Ugzh_hVzT-C3y8nLFFp4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The practical solution is to align the pilot hole with the box center so the fish contacts the cable more readily; rotate the fish tool until you feel a grab before pulling.

Q: "Why would you ever need 400 amps?? You could set up an arc welder in every room! :)" (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:Ugw7oJ9HVJj_kW3TEQR4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Recommendation: prioritize panelboard circuit spaces and proper circuit distribution, and provide dedicated branch circuits for major appliances to avoid nuisance trips. Verify service sizing with an NEC-compliant load calculation.

Q: "Also I didn't hear you mention whether you were adding a surge protector to the power circuit breaker box." (V:xTpl7WYMkcA) (Q:UgxdWjnhiSiZXylFSuF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): A plug‑on SPD replacing a two‑pole breaker is offered as a low‑cost solution. Also note NEC 2020 requires surge protection at the service equipment, so choose a compliant SPD (Type 1/Type 2).

Q: "What did you mean when you said you can't put a receptacle with your HVAC system?" (V:f7MX7PTZgRM) (Q:UgwtwHjRHhTa9L-UDMd4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Do not install receptacles, switches, or run conductors within HVAC plenum or return-air voids; route branch circuits outside the air-handling space or provide separate ducting per code. New construction generally requires ducted returns rather than using stud cavities for air return.

Q: "If a pinched wire causes heat, how can those metal clamps- clamp those wires when they enter the conduit hole in the box? Wouldn't that make a Hotspot? I know that's industry standard, but as a carpenter, it doesn't make alot of sense." (V:LdNuJksviTY) (Q:UgxoZAcjASL8r0azVR54AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Prescription): Cable connectors provide strain relief by securing the outer sheathing, not compressing conductors; properly installed connectors per manufacturer instructions prevent hotspots. Over‑tightening clamps or zip ties can deform insulation and could reduce conductor ampacity or create localized heating, but normal snug installation avoids this.
