Q: "5:26 if current is zero, then what abt cut off the neutral line, will it remain operating?😂" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:Ugzoa-pTzGR2mxrV8Cx4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): The reply advises that while a perfectly balanced load would produce zero neutral current and could theoretically tolerate an open neutral, practical unbalance causes neutral current redistribution, voltage shifts, equipment overvoltage, and safety hazards, so do not open the neutral.

Q: "The two 120 v coils that are connected together into 1 coil ( 2 hot ends and 1 neutral in the middle ) is somehow like 2 batteries ? Imagining batteries for simplification, 2 batteries together instead of 2 coils together ? Right?" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:UgwM2d58xQE86yQ-OOF4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Correction): Yes, a center‑tapped secondary can be represented as two series 120 V segments that yield 240 V end‑to‑end, but it is an AC transformer winding with a neutral center tap, not DC batteries.

Q: "14:30 the volt drop statement doesn't make any sense does it? Drop measured by a high input impedance volt meter with no other current being taken from the cable. Ohms law should tell you where you have gone wrong there...." (V:CRYnracqRjM) (Q:UgwFy4hMT5kp7bd2F-t4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Correction): The solution identifies irradiance variation (clouds) and measurement timing as the cause of the apparent voltage change; with a high‑impedance meter a PV string's Voc shifts with light, not conductor I·R drop under load.

Q: "Great video, but I have a question. In your previous video the maximum peak of the voltage falls together with the 'side' of the bar magnet. In this video it falls together with the tip of the N or S side of the magnet. What is correct?" (V:qthuFLNSrlg) (Q:UgxHuR_6bVkqwkZcH1J4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation): The creator indicates the current video's depiction of peak alignment is correct and the previous animation used a simplified model. No detailed electromagnetic derivation was provided in the replies.

# Circuit Protection Devices

A family of practitioner questions in the Conceptual type (Q4). These patterns address breakers, fuses, ground-fault and arc-fault protection, ratings, tripping, and fault response.

## At a glance

- Main subject categories: Overcurrent, Short-Circuit, and Protective Devices (54), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (9), Other/Unmapped (3)

## Common question patterns
- "Why are breakers or protective devices used for fuses and GFCI or AFCI functions?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How do GFCI devices detect and interrupt ground faults?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "How does a GFCI detect differential current?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why is required GFCI protection missing or not enforced?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why might required GFCI protection be absent despite code requirements?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why can breaker ratings exceed the main or service rating?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "What are AFCI breakers and where are they required?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are GFCI and AFCI protection not universally used on all circuits, including 240-volt circuits?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Hey David is the charge controller you have, does it have GFP and AFP so do some don't I believe you grounded that back in the garage last week which is required." (V:9DDGNp6Pcv0) (Q:UgzpqDYAOMHVLMpy8wd4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation, Prescription): The reply states NEC requires an external GFPD because these MPPT chargers lack internal ground-fault protection; the system negative should be bonded through the GFPD to earth at one location.

Q: "Awesome tutorial!!! Question: Will a 20 amp breaker trip if a 14 gauge connects several outlets?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgwqXzSBht6KZsfYiw14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): A breaker trips when load exceeds its 20 A rating. However, per NEC 240.4(D) 14 AWG conductors are limited to 15 A, so connecting 14 AWG to a 20 A breaker is noncompliant and risks thermal overload and fire even if the breaker does not immediately trip.

Q: "I don’t understand why we need a GFCI breaker and a GFCI receptacle on the same circuit" (V:g2Jfp0HyD0w) (Q:UgyDsVo3nkEXvk-Hlhl4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Either device provides ground-fault protection; which is needed depends on wiring and which downstream conductors you intend to protect. A panel GFCI protects the entire branch circuit, while a receptacle GFCI protects that receptacle and any downstream loads.

Q: "Why the AF breaker for a bedroom?" (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:UgwxUiV3IOAI3U7jC2d4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation): Reply indicates AFCI (arc-fault) protection is mandated by local building code for living spaces; bedrooms therefore receive arc-fault breakers for code compliance.

A (Prescription, Explanation): The practical solution provided is that the inverter supplies an EPS-switched outlet for critical loads during outage rather than full-house UPS continuity; achieving whole-house UPS requires additional automatic changeover hardware and appropriate earthing/grounding arrangements. Batteries in these systems are typically a ~48 V DC bus.

Q: "How is that tube venting your battery off gasing?" (V:00mOHUv3K-s) (Q:UgyIStUAwBk1v15qt1t4AaABAg)

A (Prescription, Explanation): The solution is to use matched batteries in the parallel bank and maintain them together with a smart charger/maintainer (e.g., CTEK) to minimize unequal discharge.

Q: "The small one would do wonder as a snow removal machine for personal use ! Wondering how the battery would do in a cold climate !" (V:WLOQhEmmYw8) (Q:Ugw0WUBG6vjSo4FiHwx4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The recommended mitigation is battery thermal management, use built-in heaters or heated storage and preheat batteries before operation to prevent capacity loss and reduced charge acceptance.

A (Explanation, Prescription): Explains phases are sinusoidal connection points; if one phase connection is lost, that phase is de-energized and only one line-to-line pair remains, resulting in a single-phase supply to the motor.

A (Prescription, Explanation): The float switch closes the pump control circuit and will only energize the pump if the pump has a live direct battery feed; an open manual switch or disconnected battery prevents automatic operation. Ensure the float-switch control circuit is wired to the battery with appropriate overcurrent protection and a proper negative return.

A (Correction, Explanation): The responder states the measurement is the full coil (transformer secondary) line-to-line potential of 240 V, which supplies 240 V loads like ranges.

## Common question patterns

- "How do parallel branch loads and a GFCI affect current cancellation and neutral-current imbalance?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why not using always the thickest wire for safety reasons. Then you're ALWAYS good to go. Or is that too expensive?" (V:EYcXtWHMKqw) (Q:UgzHim7N29NjYxnvRtF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Explanation): Match conductor ampacity to the overcurrent device rating per NEC; oversizing adds cost and complicates pulling and derating without improving overcurrent protection.

Q: "I didnt understand how you select grouping factor for ID Calculation why you take 0.82 ??? please explain" (V:098UloW6xfk) (Q:UgyMDVcXDQ-ScXfMqoF4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): The grouping factor 0.82 was taken from the BS 7671 tabulated correction factors corresponding to a 50°C ambient temperature and applied to the Id calculation. The responder also indicates the video shows values for other ambient temperatures.

Q: "Can incorrectly connected wires increase electricity bills? 🔌💵" (V:UBERduCp3Wo) (Q:UgxoOoBzIIBaO753D7N4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Prescription): Incorrect conductor connections will not change measured energy unless they introduce extra load current, leakage, or short-circuit losses; overcurrent devices should clear faults before sustained increased consumption occurs.

Q: "*> Why, you did Demand factor and Diversity factor both multiply. is it correct. *> Always Diversity factor should be in more than one. also Demand factor always should be in less than one. but you were did something please clear me. *> D.…" (V:IebflvdLVvM) (Q:UgwWVKSHILkapyBkf2J4AaABAg)
A (Explanation): The best reply distinguishes diversity (used to estimate consumption by load type) from demand/load factor (used in actual load-sheet calculations) and notes the template uses averaged diversity values.

## Common question patterns

- "Why does ampacity use different temperature columns and load factors?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why is the electrical installation being inspected or documented this way?" (asked by 3 commenters)

- "Why assume the measurements were not performed by the contractor?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "What device detects electrical power or wiring conditions?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why do you go off the 70⁰ column and not the 90⁰ I'm assuming it is because your lugs are rated at 75⁰ but I just want to verify." (V:BfYHDkMAINM) (Q:Ugz6gbuvIrC-3DgPAQF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Perform ampacity calculations using the 90°C ampacity column for adjustment factors and derating, then select the conductor and overcurrent device based on the 75°C termination rating to comply with NEC.

Q: "I have outdoor outlets with GFI. There is a small light on the outlets that are green sometimes and off most of the time. The outlets work even if the light is off. What is this light for. Thanks" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:UgwknOVMti9SvB-XfsN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Test the GFCI using its built-in test/reset buttons to verify tripped-state and downstream continuity; indicator LEDs vary by manufacturer and some are EOL indicators.

Q: "Can I ask why you do insulation test on the electrical board to find which circuit is faulty and then proceed with continuity tests and not insulation tests? Just hope you can help me understand better, and thanks for the great video" (V:BK6ykUkJ-8A) (Q:UgzxozJfhpk490awdaB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Continuity measurement is used after isolation to measure fault impedance and distinguish direct low-Ω shorts from high-impedance leakage that insulation resistance testing indicates. It provides diagnostic detail for localization and repair planning.

Q: "With respect to neutral, does the hot wire swing 0-110 or +/- 55 Volts? Is there a 0 Volt reference in residential circuits?" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:UgzJdosXPFVgE9wKWgZ4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Correction): The best reply indicates the hot conductor is a sinusoid about neutral and that peak amplitude equals RMS×√2, so an RMS reading of 110 V corresponds to approximately ±165 V peak on a scope. It also contrasts voltmeter (RMS) versus oscilloscope (peak) measurements.

Q: "I found that I only have two black wires on my switch. Why is that?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgwJdjT33uXIhqkMVxd4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Prescription): The reply explains the switch interrupts the hot conductor; the two black wires are the line (hot feed) and load (switched hot) tied to the switch terminals. Neutrals are typically not connected to the switch and remain spliced in the box, while grounds are attached to the device.

A family of practitioner questions in the Diagnostic type (Q5). Patterns concern GFCI or residual-current devices that trip, fail to reset, lose power, or provide incorrect protection.

## Common question patterns

- "How can line and load conductors be identified after removing a GFCI?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "What causes an RCD to trip from a neutral-to-earth fault?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "So I have one of these in my garage. And it seems to be acting as a breaker when I use the other outlets in my garage. The gfci trips when I have a block heater for my diesel truck. . I feel like I should be able to run so much more off on…" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:UgyMe7x_0C_Rd2TAnN14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The practical troubleshooting step is to isolate the circuit by removing downstream loads and retest the block heater to determine if the GFCI trips due to a faulty heater/cord or downstream leakage. Replies also warn that high-inrush or welding equipment can cause nuisance trips.

Q: "I’m not a home owner and I live in 50+ year apartment complex. In the living room I have an outlet that only works on the bottom socket Don’t know why. And one outlet in the bathroom and one in the kitchen has a weird outlet- reset button.…" (V:g2Jfp0HyD0w) (Q:Ugy4YTFdsHBDIxTyfDh4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Prescription): GFCI trips on ground-faults and must be reset after the fault is cleared; outlets downstream may be fed through a single GFCI. A receptacle only powering the bottom outlet indicates an open neutral/half-switched or reversed wiring that a qualified person should correct.

Q: "When I replaced my GFCI in my bathroom due to no power there were 4 wires going into the line side . 2 hot and 2 neutral. Can you explain why it's hooked up this way and why I still have no power" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:UgwCgqsVeFe6e0TP69B4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Hedged speculation): The recommended remediation is to place a single hot and single neutral on the GFCI LINE terminals and pigtail the supply to feed the other conductors. The commenter attributes the 4-wire landing to bypassing downstream protection but could not diagnose the continued loss of power.

Q: "PE I installed a light/heat/ fan combo I had the fan/light on the load side of the GFCI kept tripping," (V:eJBet9kofcM) (Q:Ugx67EHJVLwQgDm10AZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction): The recommended solution is to place the unit on a dedicated branch circuit sized for its load, verify the unit's running current, and use 12 AWG conductors on a 20 A breaker to avoid overloads and nuisance trips.

Q: "Upgrading from 2 pong to a 3 pong gfci; My old house had a yellow and a white cable bonded together I split them apart with yellow on silver screw and white on ground screw, and black on gold screw, the weird part is that it works but now…" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgzanZPx7zpcw9Nkjb94AaABAg)
A (Correction, Prescription, Explanation): The reply states the white conductor was improperly used as a grounding conductor, creating an objectionable ground and hazard, and recommends reverting the wiring and contacting a professional electrician.

Q: "Thank you for this very helpful video Scott! Would a bad circuit breaker be the reason that several outlets have no electricity? Also, how would I know which circuit breaker corresponds to a certain outlet or switch? Thank you for any help…" (V:bGZVILwbyLo) (Q:UgxRZ5TeBmXJRzVk5Pt4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Test branch-circuit continuity by applying a known load and operating the overcurrent device to see if the load de-energizes; alternatively use an electronic circuit tracer/breaker finder. Also inspect receptacle terminations for loose/backstab connections that can create open hot/neutral conditions.

Q: "I have power coming from inside outlet to outside. I have power inside. No power outside, i have power at the screws, but no power in the outlet. Ive chaged eires to different configurations. Nothing works. My brother thinks ground is the…" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:UgzITMMDKD8H330BaYR4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The reply indicates the outdoor receptacle is likely defective. Replacing the receptacle should restore downstream power.

Q: "I have several outlets not working. How do I determine which is the bad outlet? Another issue: I want to override my ballasts in my flourescent light fixtures w led lights. Can I do that w the daisy chain fluorescents fixtures installed in…" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgyGP3X7o_tpe6rvEpN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction): The reply instructs to find a known-live receptacle, identify and open the associated breaker, confirm the circuit is de-energized, then test downstream receptacles to locate the fault. It also advises not to bypass ballasts, replace the luminaire or use an LED-compatible driver/fixture.

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Please may you expand on the very last point you made: if power is flowing from hot through the ground, and it's very low (think you said current because high resistance?) What would happen in this case? It won't trip the breaker, so will…" (V:P-W42tk-fWc) (Q:UgwyToTJHLd9DIoTXM54AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): An isolated hot-to-ground fault into a single earth electrode typically produces only a few amps due to earth electrode resistance, so overcurrent devices usually won't operate; however the electrode and nearby ground can become energized, producing hazardous step/touch potentials and local heating. Conversely, if the earth electrode is bonded into the neutral/ground system the fault current will…

Q: "If I disconnect the neutral line wire and use a non voltage contact tester it will indicate its hot?" (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:Ugy16eXHhrvglZVPaah4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Non‑contact voltage testers can produce false positives; use a multimeter (or clamp ammeter for current checks) to verify voltage and current and test both hot and neutral conductors.

Q: "I have bare copper grounds in my house... I still get shocked. I have to shut off the main breaker to the whole house just to prevent from getting shocked by the ground." (V:bGZVILwbyLo) (Q:UgzXAiytDMya3dGjz8Z4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Referral): Advice identifies faulty grounding/bonding at the main panel, check the panel bonding screw, neutral-to-ground bonding, grounding electrode conductor and connections to grounding rod/water pipe. Engage a qualified electrician to repair grounding electrode conductor, bonding jumpers, and correct dryer receptacle wiring to code.

Q: "So please what happens when the mango tree is cut" (V:uNmFVhomJHw) (Q:Ugx8UYxwEN48mDzh3pZ4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Prescription): Removal of the tree can increase local soil resistivity by reducing moisture and organic content, which may raise earth electrode resistance. Verify with an earth resistance test and remediate with additional electrodes, improved backfill, or re-siting if resistance exceeds acceptable limits.

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Hello, We have an old boat with a 351 windsor inboard. The gauges work when the key is turned, but go off when we start and run the engine. Any idea what this may be?" (V:ycTi1SLmods) (Q:UgzhrmacUacZBkXn-4F4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Referral, Hedged speculation): The reply diagnoses a voltage drop during starter cranking as the likely cause and recommends professional inspection to trace supply, switching, and grounding integrity.

Q: "I wired it exactly like this to a T and get power to the ports and switches but accessories aren’t turning on, you know what it could be?? Thanks" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:UgxqTJ5Wjnmtex88bl94AaABAg)
A (Prescription): Verify each accessory has a continuous battery negative return to the negative/ground bus and that the accessory positive is connected to the switch output terminal, not the switch input. Check switch terminal pinouts and continuity with a multimeter and inspect crimped ring terminals and heat‑shrinked joints.

Q: "I dig it. Make some more videos. I have a pontoon I'm trying to rebuild. The dumbass B4 me jumped every wire 15 times. I have no idea what goes to what. Can you help?" (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:UgzVakcTd0kb2B8ZPcd4AaABAg)
A (Prescription): The recommended solution is a full rewire: remove the existing harness and install a new, correctly routed and terminated wiring system to ensure proper circuit identification and reliability.

# Workmanship and Installation Quality

## Common question patterns
- "Why was the work performed or presented in this manner?" (asked by 176 commenters)
- "Why is meticulous, neat panelboard workmanship worth the additional time and cost?" (asked by 45 commenters)
- "Why were safety loops or cable routing arranged this way?" (asked by 13 commenters)
- "Why were conductors not twisted before installing the wire connector?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why was the installation left untidy instead of following neat workmanship practices?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Is a disorganized panelboard worse when tracing and maintaining circuits than an organized panelboard?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "How could the finished pendant assembly be better than the reference photograph if the builder had never built one before?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why should a customer object when a paid electrician takes extra time to produce meticulous workmanship?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Negative connection should be given to earthing....😅I found fault in your circuit... reply me" (V:H71ZjTO_5_8) (Q:UgwFh4qLE9EOEQ2s8bh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction, Explanation): Recommendation to rewire the control as a ground-side (low-side) switch so the relay and fuse handle the horn current; acknowledges chassis as battery negative/common ground.

Q: "If I had to cut a large hole as you did, I would use a nail plate instead of mounting the conduit to the back of the hole as it could be damaged by a nail from outside. What are your thoughts?" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:Ugx75DZtlpdAMwPl71p4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription): The reply confirms nail/safety plates are code-required to protect raceways. It also notes EMT is typically centered in the stud and the video shows that installation technique.

Q: "What does it matter how clean it is? Its all going to be covered up anyway." (V:PrJlFlL9I84) (Q:UgxuShGALEbgZRxyEv94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Recommendation: use planning, basic layout measurement (laser or chalk line), and installation experience to produce neat, code-compliant rough-in without significant extra time.

Q: "Wait, are you doing all the installation straight on the enclosure itself??? No installation panel???" (V:0eF0iZ2YWj4) (Q:UgwgCv_QORGL2WzAocJ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The accepted practice is either tray/back-of-enclosure mounting or internal mounting on a panelboard/mounting plate. Maintain required IP rating and follow local/regional installation regulations to avoid ingress/inspection issues.

# Conduit Routing Bends and Protection

A family of practitioner questions in the Practice justification and challenge type (Q6). These patterns question conduit paths, bends, fittings, supports, seals, and protection during installation.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 186 (11.5% of all Practice justification and challenge questions)
- Never received any reply: 123 (66.1%)
- Replied but unresolved: 16
- Answered: 47 (answer rate among the 63 replied questions: 74.6%)
- Question activity by year: 2018: 1, 2019: 5, 2020: 8, 2021: 47, 2022: 49, 2023: 37, 2024: 37, 2025: 2
- Main subject categories: Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (164), Other/Unmapped (8), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (6)

## Common question patterns
- "Why was conduit or nonmetallic-sheathed cable used instead of the other wiring method?" (asked by 22 commenters)
- "Why was metal or EMT conduit used instead of a simpler wiring method?" (asked by 12 commenters)
- "Why was metallic conduit used instead of PVC or another nonmetallic raceway?" (asked by 10 commenters)
- "Why was a bushing, grommet, or locking clamp omitted at the cable or conduit entry?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why were conduit bends or elbows omitted?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why were conduit runs left discontinuous, leaving cable exposed?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why were conduit runs not connected to boxes with elbows or fittings?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why were elbows, couplings, or connectors omitted from conduit runs?" (asked by 4 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why not use a big pull box, then run a few conduits for the main panel. This allows for clean and future work (if needed)." (V:l-gOTyql6RM) (Q:Ugx_i0eD988iIJQBvzB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The clear solution: conduit with multiple current-carrying conductors requires ampacity derating, so plan ampacity per NEC; using individual NMSC/NM cables preserves full conductor rating but limits future pull/access.

Q: "I’d be interested in seeing your conduit bending skills. I guess you don’t need box offsets using those straps. I’ve honestly never seen anyone use a coupling to make a box connector like you did. Sure it’ll work, We just two lock nuts her…" (V:rvUlnrCuzew) (Q:UgyvyA7EoNGa5U-zJyh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Use a compression connector combined with an internal locknut and an insulating washer to protect conductors at the entry; note the washer can fall out so control pull tension and feed to prevent abrasion.

Q: "For a European it is odd to see wire that is not pulled through a tube. Having tubes in the wall make changes easier. https://simonakerfelt.files.wordpress.com/2014/03/img_20140206_133152.jpg" (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:Ugygj0NKGnIRyjlRGT14AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Experience report, Code or authority citation): The recommended solution presented is to run conductors in conduit/tubing in-wall per code to reduce chafing and enable future rewiring. Surface-mounted raceways are offered as a practical alternative in wood-frame or retrofit scenarios, subject to inspector approval.

Q: "All EMT??... Extra money and labor cost on so many levels.. Plus, the cost of EMT is not cheap and as of 2018 a cost of 10' EMT is worth around $3.25.. Oh, and don't forget the fittings.." (V:Z7Akm2gLxz0) (Q:UgwDzc3AqTCof_znNX94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): The technical reply recommends EMT for long-term durability, improved grounding/bonding with metal boxes, and to enable THHN conductors with higher ampacity in conditioned spaces, offsetting some material costs.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "Why aren't you using Romex or MC n a shed it's wood structure emt is overkill just way to much work" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:Ugz910gjLyLRXekDrUx4AaABAg)

# Conductor Routing and Physical Protection

A family of practitioner questions in the Practice justification and challenge type (Q6). These patterns question cable placement, securing, penetration protection, slack, and routing choices.

## At a glance

## Common question patterns
- "Why are service loops or extra conductor slack provided or omitted?" (asked by 33 commenters)
- "Why was a purpose-built pulling grip or sock not used for pulling conductors?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why were stud-penetration protection plates and related cable-protection measures omitted?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Why were conductors pulled only after the conduit run was completed?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why was a pull string used instead of another method for pulling conductors through the conduit?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why were cables or conductors left with excessive slack or coils instead of being trimmed?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why was the conduit or cable routed under or outside the vehicle instead of being protected inside?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are cables stapled inside wall cavities instead of being installed according to the commenter’s New Zealand practice?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why are those two 14/2 wires to the left,not coming straight through the flior?Why are the on a angle?" (V:l-gOTyql6RM) (Q:UgyJniSMjNvk6Py_a3d4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): The reply prescribes securing the NM-B 14/2 conductors with staples so they lie flat, correcting routing and preventing displacement.

Q: "Whats wrong with service loops?? Im not a resi guy but when im rewiring stuff on my house i hate the fucker 50 years ago that didnt leave any service loops. In industrial we generally leave some slack to work with." (V:PrJlFlL9I84) (Q:Ugxcnk7QbZz1g-1_6Tl4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report): The consensus solution is to perform branch-circuit replacement when NM-B exceeds expected life (~25 years) rather than manipulating brittle service loops; inaccessible runs may require drywall removal.

Q: "No slack on the wire at the boxes? This will bite you in the ass when the drywaller cuts your wires with his roto zip...6 inches of extra is all you need, I would never do this!" (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:UgzpP2PSXKyAhZ8A_d94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): The replies reference a 2020 code update allowing an 18-inch service loop when the conductor is secured within 12 inches of the box. Absent that securing or in some jurisdictions, lack of slack may fail inspection.

Q: "A question for you: why did you use separate wires and not a Romex, is it easier, or is it maybe some code requirement?" (V:Frt0vJ4k15g) (Q:UgzffavtiOIIAEamUA14AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation): The reply indicates the code restricts NM (Romex) in conduit to short runs (~10 ft) and that individual conductors must be identified, so separate conductors were used instead of Romex.

## Common question patterns

- "Why were cable-pulling and conductor-preparation methods used instead of simpler methods?" (asked by 9 commenters)

- "Why was the conduit or cable bending method questioned?" (asked by 6 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "first of all, you need to choose the right drill size! there is no need to drill 5x bigger hole just for one wire! I am seeing all the time same mistake everyone does, - people are buying 1" drill bit and do not care. Why?" (V:HTrsF20jA80) (Q:UgyWEzNDrSbF57ir3rd4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation): The recommended practical solution from the replies is to use a 1" bore where permitted by code because it facilitates pulls and protects NM sheathing; however, some field practitioners prefer smaller bores when sufficient for the conductors to minimize removed stud material.

Q: "Uses forks and straps to move the attachments. Considering the loader has hydraulic quick attachment feature seems it would have been much simpler and faster just to drop the forks and couple the attachments directly to the loader to move…" (V:WLOQhEmmYw8) (Q:UgxrWR3IfspBes8Jagh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Reorienting the attachments to the correct position enables hydraulic quick-attach coupling; swapping can be completed in about three minutes from the operator cab.

Q: "why not use a pipe cutter ?" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:UgxB6CVTLtuAUk9glip4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report): The recommended technique: rotate the pipe cutter until nearly through, then flex the EMT to snap at the score line. When executed properly this produces a clean edge and can avoid reaming and internal burrs.

Q: "I question the reliability of this demo when the person demonstrating is using an impact driver/drill as a hammer to remove knockouts." (V:9P9_AieEFEI) (Q:Ugxs3x2UoAWAodmZHHB4AaABAg)
A (Experience report, Correction): A licensed electrician explicitly confirms the demonstrated knockout removal technique as proper. No further technical explanation or NEC citation was provided in the replies.

family-q6-f05.chunkText:
# Splicing and Termination Practices

A family of practitioner questions in the Practice justification and challenge type (Q6). These patterns question conductor preparation, splices, connectors, tape, crimps, lugs, and termination methods.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 128 (7.9% of all Practice justification and challenge questions)
- Never received any reply: 86 (67.2%)
- Replied but unresolved: 19
- Answered: 23 (answer rate among the 42 replied questions: 54.8%)
- Question activity by year: 2020: 9, 2021: 20, 2022: 34, 2023: 28, 2024: 27, 2025: 10
- Main subject categories: Other/Unmapped (82), Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (15), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (10)

## Common question patterns
- "Why was antioxidant compound not applied to aluminum conductor terminations?" (asked by 31 commenters)
- "Why were pigtails or unusual splices used instead of a simpler termination?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Why was torque verification not shown or performed?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why are screw-type connectors used instead of push-in connectors?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why were wire nuts not used for the conductor connections?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was pigtailing used instead of through-wiring at the receptacles?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are lever-nut connectors recommended while stab-in receptacle terminals are discouraged even though both clamp bare conductors?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why are the equipment grounding conductors wrapped around the ungrounded conductor instead of being left separate?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Clean install but one question. Why did you not use NoLox on the aluminum wire where it connects to the transfer switch and gennny?" (V:_IDluE3fEoc) (Q:Ugw-bx_Lw-9rjXfmY7Z4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation, Correction): The respondent states that modern aluminum alloy conductors reduce oxidation risk and NoLox is not required by the NEC, but he applies it when available and recognizes some AHJ mandates.

Q: "Why would you use dielectric grease? This isn't electronics; anti-oxidant compound is what you should have used." (V:9GQLaZ-ywRU) (Q:Ugx5kizmeoUQ0_GFbG54AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Use a NOL-OX anti-oxidant on aluminum terminations when required, because it promotes conductive contact; dielectric (silicone) grease is non-conductive and only provides moisture exclusion. Modern aluminum alloys and code updates may affect requirements.

Q: "Johb, what is your thought on taping all pigtail connections for extra stability?" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:Ugz5AKWiVYR68ePLgJB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): The recommended practice is not to tape wire-nut pigtail splices because proper strip length and correct wire-nut installation eliminate exposed conductors; tape can cause slacking that loosens the splice and makes future rework more difficult.

Q: "I’m no electrician, but that is not the grounded wire that you .2 with the white tape on it that’s the neutral coming from the pole. Do you know what you’re talking about?" (V:ZQOTvsXtrKo) (Q:Ugxe5Qq_VSzsY33Qrdh4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation): The neutral is the grounded conductor in a single-phase 120/240 V service and should not be conflated with the equipment grounding conductor; correct terminology and identification are emphasized.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "Why not wagos? so much better" (V:ocj_kdHv1_I) (Q:UgxkMSETYkeKIBe4lxF4AaABAg)

# Conductor Sizing and Electrical Calculations

A family of practitioner questions in the Practice justification and challenge type (Q6). These patterns question conductor selection, ratings, load calculations, voltage, phasing, and circuit configuration.

## At a glance

- Never received any reply: 66 (55.9%)
- Replied but unresolved: 23
- Answered: 29 (answer rate among the 52 replied questions: 55.8%)
- Question activity by year: 2018: 2, 2019: 3, 2020: 10, 2021: 27, 2022: 34, 2023: 20, 2024: 14, 2025: 8
- Main subject categories: Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (71), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (23), Code Interpretation, Safety, and Field Operations (12)

## Common question patterns
- "Why were aluminum conductors used instead of copper conductors?" (asked by 16 commenters)
- "Why were conductors sized or routed this way?" (asked by 11 commenters)
- "Why were 12 AWG conductors used instead of 14 AWG conductors?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "Why were larger conductors used for lighting circuits instead of smaller conductors?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Why were 12 AWG conductors used for lighting circuits instead of 14 AWG conductors?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why were conductors or breakers supplied from only one phase?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why was 14 AWG cable used for a bathroom branch circuit instead of 12 AWG cable?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was the conductor phasing or phase marking done this way?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "why 12/2 ? u need it just for Kitchen Counter Recepticles.... u wasted money" (V:f7MX7PTZgRM) (Q:UgwmQBjhId1zaCCu6Y14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Recommendation: use 12/2 (12 AWG) on kitchen small-appliance branch circuits per NEC; ordinary living-area receptacles may be 14/2 on 15A circuits. Note 12/2 increases box fill and requires appropriate box volume.

Q: "Why #14 romex?! We only run #12 home runs to each room" (V:l-gOTyql6RM) (Q:Ugxl4L_RwzhJ_VdgISt4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): Reply implies 14 AWG is used for circuits that do not require 20 A. Per NEC, 14 AWG is limited to 15 A (NEC 240.4(D)), while 12 AWG is for 20 A branch circuits.

Q: "how big is the building? thats big power. also why run 3 phase to the office?" (V:qI8jfmP8raA) (Q:UgwzZHNGo8sqs6D__7F4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Use single-pole breakers in the three-phase panel to feed regular office lighting and receptacles, which can reduce conductor counts. Confirm system voltage (e.g., 208/120 vs 480/277) and locate any required step-down transformer appropriately.

Q: "Why not run 14/3,it's leas expensive and easier to work with?As far as removing the wire from the center of the roll,it's easier to roll it out from the outside and step on the wire as your waking it out.It keeps the wire flat." (V:1D5OqJ5SF_I) (Q:Ugz68p2HwNiNPkuDeyV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): You must maintain 12 AWG conductors on a 20 A circuit; downgrading conductors forces a 15 A overcurrent device. Use 12/3 for a 20 A fan/light split control circuit.

Q: "Why are You running 12awg for lights?" (V:dgmwJWLs084) (Q:UgzOhywWimpoUHsCQWd4AaABAg)

## Common question patterns
- "Why were service panels installed outdoors instead of indoors?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "Why was a subpanel installed instead of distributing circuits from the existing main panel?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why was the panelboard mounted unusually high?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why was the panelboard wiring disorganized instead of neatly routed?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Did the installation remove the old sealing putty before applying new putty at the service entrance or panel penetration?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was the panelboard not installed with the main breaker at the bottom?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was the electric meter placed on the street-facing side?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was the service panel installed at that height or location?" (asked by 2 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Why do you have that external panel? Speaking from what I've seen in Iowa, I've never seen outside panel boxes, like that. I've always only seen the electrical panel on the interior of the home, hence my asking." (V:xTpl7WYMkcA) (Q:UgxzdFM4GhZ4zl0MXq94AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation, Experience report): The exterior service disconnect is now required by NEC 230.85 in many jurisdictions; exterior mounting also simplifies wiring for outdoor loads, generators, and subpanel feeds.

Q: "Hi...been bending since 1985...nice...why didn't you use flex or bx...just asking? 🤔" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:Ugz9YvruN2-rScZiVHx4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation, Prescription): The reply states the Fire Marshal prohibits general use of flex/BX due to gaps in the armor allowing smoke and fire penetration; short luminaire loops may be allowed.

Q: "So you have to run outside to turn off if somethings wrong inside??!! That's kinda dumb" (V:qI8jfmP8raA) (Q:Ugz6m09CjMxG9imZERx4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Prescription, Explanation): The solution: interior branch-circuit breakers and panel main disconnects provide normal isolation, while the exterior disconnect is an emergency/FD-accessible device for rapid de-energization.

Q: "Haven’t you learned anything? Why are you putting your utilities on the outside of your house?" (V:xTpl7WYMkcA) (Q:UgybNyGSagjG5wRjzqp4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Recommend routing service entrance conductors through the wall to place the panelboard inside, reducing the number of air barrier penetrations to a single larger conductor entry for easier sealing and access.

A family of practitioner questions in the Practice justification and challenge type (Q6). These patterns question building assemblies, concrete, framing, penetrations, equipment placement, and trade sequencing.

## Common question patterns
- "Why was the concrete work performed this way?" (asked by 14 commenters)
- "Why were extra concrete deliveries or quantities accepted instead of ordering only the required amount?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "Why was the reinforcing steel or mesh left without adequate support?" (asked by 8 commenters)
- "Why were structural members drilled, cut, or penetrated for electrical work?" (asked by 6 commenters)
- "Does using factory-cut structural insulated panel wiring prevent unplanned field changes?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why was only the required amount of concrete ordered instead of extra material to avoid a shortfall?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are exterior concrete masonry units offset?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why are horizontal wall blocks, or noggins, absent from the wall cavities shown?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Please can somebody explain to me why the electric goes in before mechanical? I mean, imo, electric is much more flexible thant hvac and if something hvac related changes the electrician will have to visit again?" (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:UgyeWYB2m6_faG9GxKN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): The recommended trade sequence is plumbing, then HVAC, then electrical to avoid conflicts between ducts/pipes and electrical routing. However, practical scheduling and pre-marking by HVAC can alter on-site order.

Q: "Do you put noggings in your studs? Seemed to be a lot of deflection when he was drilling them," (V:VUh_yHc6C2c) (Q:UgznxGDHe61XTQ9EZDl4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): The accepted solution: blocking (noggings) is not typically used to prevent drilling deflection, it's a fireblocking requirement on walls over 10 ft, not a structural measure.

Q: "Did you allow for the logs expanding in autumn/winter?" (V:stQpNIZlhxA) (Q:Ugz7luUPCEUOKvaCNMd4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): The practical solution offered is to fit expansion couplers on affected runs. Also monitor moisture-affected timber because PVC and wood have comparable expansion/contraction behavior.

Q: "when you read up on the sip system it says everything is pre cut including the electrical so why the hell is he cutting into the walls if everything is done for the electrical from the factory?" (V:E6hE1-OOGyY) (Q:UghIuKITQdZHAngCoAEC)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Specify outlet and box locations on plans prior to SIP fabrication so the manufacturer precuts chases and box openings. Factory precuts reduce field labor, though additional field boxes or adjustments remain common.

Unanswered example (no reply ever came):
Q: "Not putting chicken mesh? Love from India🇮🇳" (V:cvop70SnKAA) (Q:UgyMg2FBGvVFUM48dPV4AaABAg)

Q: "Why didn't you just leave the existing receptacle and add the new one? Would have been less work." (V:Jpu-3zB8Pqs) (Q:Ugx1hbpmGvfSDaPnqYR4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Explanation): The NEC regulates branch-circuit load rather than a fixed receptacle count. For bathrooms, provide the required 20 A branch circuit and GFCI protection while verifying conductor ampacity, box fill, and grounding/bonding.

Q: "It would be nice to see the dishwasher receptacle under the sink so it can be plugged in." (V:J3jotQFZ5vA) (Q:Ugzi3bxP--v5i1Vdm3Z4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): Installer recommends hardwiring but will install an adjustable under-sink box to separate AFCI at the panel from GFCI at the sink to prevent nuisance tripping, per inspector guidance.

Q: "Why don't you make up your boxes on rough in? I like to do it on rough cause contractors never give me much time come final time" (V:J3jotQFZ5vA) (Q:Ugz3LlcHuicKaA7ZolV4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation): The clear solution: device makeup timing is governed by inspector acceptance, not NEC mandate. Waiting until trim-out prevents paint contamination of terminations and protects luminaire caps; cleaning is a workaround.

Q: "I never understood why you wouldn't cover that with a removable panel so if need be you could repair stuff ." (V:cvop70SnKAA) (Q:UgzxqNskWdvkmvOub7F4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The suggested solution is to use conduit with an access/pull point so wires can be pulled or replaced via the access panel without re-exposing wall grooves.

## Common question patterns
- "Why were neutral and equipment grounding conductors bonded or terminated together?" (asked by 13 commenters)
- "Why were the grounding conductors or bonding connections arranged this way?" (asked by 11 commenters)
- "Why was the equipment grounding conductor connected away from the expected adjacent or higher terminal on the grounding bus?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why was the grounding conductor routed directly to the panel or through a separate penetration instead of through the meter base or enclosure?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why is the neutral bonded to the grounding bus in this panel?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why were two grounding electrodes installed instead of one?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why are equipment grounding conductors in Vancouver connected with a pigtail and wire connector instead of being twisted with one conductor left under the device terminal?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why are ungrounded two-prong plugs used instead of grounded three-prong plugs?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Where is your Ground Buss ? You do not Bond the Neutral and Ground on a Sub Panel." (V:-nBDlutORiQ) (Q:UgxGMXrlOJ-L4U4s_px4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Prescription, Code or authority citation): Because this is a main service panel, a ground bus must be provided and bonded to the neutral bus (main bonding jumper) as the service bonding point; follow NEC 250 and local amendments.

Q: "No Nolox on the primary cable connections.There dry and will corrode. In my county the Inspector will ding you for that. And you say first time you connect ground and neutral together? Really. Where is a neutral coming from when you don't…" (V:ZQOTvsXtrKo) (Q:Ugw32NHxAnolcAUVtiR4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The replies state NoAlox/anti-oxide compounds are for aluminum conductors, not copper, and that modern AA-8000 aluminum alloy reduced the historic need for NoAlox. For corrosive environments, sealed stainless enclosures (NEMA 4X) are recommended and limited compound use on large AL terminations is optional.

Q: "If is just 1 grounding rod, why did you get 2? Just curious." (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:Ugzak-Ff6HaHEXTkWOl4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation, Hedged speculation): The consensus answer is that code typically requires two ground rods spaced approximately six feet. Local AHJ adoption and ground-electrode resistance (affected by soil resistivity) determine if a single rod is acceptable.

Q: "47:23 Hey Lauren! Amazing video learnt a lot and doing simmilar set up, got one question - why you connect chasis ground to the front of the lynx, is there specific reason? Coz just in the manual it says the dedicated area is in the midle…" (V:3Gr3rr4cPQQ) (Q:Ugz0ElXc6RS-m_Ht7SZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): The practical solution: landing the chassis ground at the Lynx front busbar is acceptable and was chosen to preserve a spare negative terminal for future circuit expansion; no functional difference compared to the central ground point.

# Alternative Wiring Methods

A family of practitioner questions in the Practice justification and challenge type (Q6). These patterns compare conduit, cable, raceway, concealed wiring, and other installation methods.

## At a glance
- Questions in this family: 61 (3.8% of all Practice justification and challenge questions)
- Never received any reply: 30 (49.2%)

- Answered: 19 (answer rate among the 31 replied questions: 61.3%)
- Question activity by year: 2013: 1, 2014: 1, 2015: 2, 2017: 1, 2019: 2, 2020: 3, 2021: 19, 2022: 16, 2023: 5, 2024: 9, 2025: 2
- Main subject categories: Conductors, Raceway, and Physical Routing (56), Power Distribution and Service Infrastructure (3), Other/Unmapped (1)

## Common question patterns
- "Why was MC cable used instead of NM cable?" (asked by 4 commenters)
- "Why was EMT run to the box instead of terminating MC cable directly at the box?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why was the MC cable transitioned to EMT at the electrical box instead of being routed directly to the box?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why were conductors installed without protective raceway?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why were PVC conduit joints installed without solvent cement?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was the EMT raceway threaded?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are baseboard wiring ducts not commonly installed in residential houses?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why are conductors fastened to the ICF framing instead of being routed through embedded plastic conduit?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Any idea what the justification could be for requiring conduit here (as opposed to MC/AC)?" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:UgymgdlvWiXBIEwNn6Z4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): The primary justification given is that raceways permit conductor pullability/replacement and comply with local AHJ restrictions against nonmetallic/PVC or NM cable for fire/toxic-fume reasons; conduit also provides equipment grounding continuity and can mitigate EMI.

Q: "Why would you do such a thing like that? Just run the mc to the box you dont need emt for that. I am a licensed Master electrician for the last 30 yrs." (V:HhwEwbgZFA4) (Q:Ugh-p8JycNIxzHgCoAEC)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): The practical solution: route MC cable overhead and then use an EMT-to-MC transition for the surface-mounted conduit run to improve surface appearance and provide a conduit finish. This is presented as a standard field method.

Q: "Why did you have to run conduit inside of walls instead of romex? Im in Ohio and thought conduit is not required inside of walls." (V:2noHrGkGuhQ) (Q:Ugw5bpken74WvhjO-Gl4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Experience report, Correction): The installation used MC (metal-clad) per the job prints/specs, providing greater mechanical protection and rodent resistance than NM-B (Romex); local AHJ/municipal rules can also mandate conduit.

Q: "why does everything seem flimsy and plastic. why didn't you use actual conduit connected directly to boxes? metal may be out of style, but it's still a great material. wires can get hot. what happens when plastics get hot? a good reason to…" (V:wsJONukJlLI) (Q:UgxGfiZDgTxoehyjrtR4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): The reply argues that PVC's thermal limit (≈210°C) exceeds the maximum conductor operating temperature (~70°C) required by code, so properly sized conductors and overcurrent protection keep plastic ducts within safe temperature margins. However, mechanical protection and fault containment considerations may still justify metallic conduit in high-risk installations.

# Protective Devices and Arrangements

A family of practitioner questions in the Practice justification and challenge type (Q6). These patterns question breakers, fuses, ground-fault protection, arc-fault protection, and hazardous energized conditions.

## At a glance

## Common question patterns
- "Why were fuses or fusible links used instead of circuit breakers?" (asked by 12 commenters)
- "Why was GFCI protection omitted or not required by the inspection?" (asked by 7 commenters)
- "Why was a larger generator selected instead of a smaller generator for the home?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was downstream GFCI protection not provided?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why was the GFCI line/load termination distinction not explained?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why were surge-protection devices omitted?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Why are screw-type input fuses used instead of cartridge fuses or a circuit breaker?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why did the video omit the NFPA 70, NEC 210.12 required arc-fault protection?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "Do you really need the fuse box with the amp breaker and the switches (which already has protection.) This seems like overkill to me." (V:5qaA_0eDQa0) (Q:UgxwI6mCt7VYYT1cAlZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Use a dedicated, appropriately rated circuit breaker for the trolling motor and individual branch fuses in a fuse block for accessories. Branch fuses provide overcurrent/fire protection that switch internal protection may not replace.

Q: "Why did you still use three screw fuses / melting fuses in the control cabinet instead of modern circuit breakers? What are their advantages?" (V:wsJONukJlLI) (Q:UgzdaqTuhIPxm7rUZyZ4AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): Fuses provide predictable time-current characteristics and inherent coordination/selectivity with upstream protection, and are less prone to electronic/mechanical failure modes in breakers. Tradeoffs include single-use replacement after operation and lack of an integral reset.

Q: "Why wouldn’t the neutral from the neutral bar and the active from the top go into the bottom terminals, it would work the same won’t it ..!" (V:qRE58D0Zh_k) (Q:UgxIbwKb9cQsQCE0Qv14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Hedged speculation): Reversing line/load can cause the internal test resistor or trip circuit to overheat and fail. Verify manufacturer-specified line/load orientation because some RCDs are bidirectional.

Q: "Why would you not want the GFCI to protect the downstream devices?" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:UgyFN0ZSno_9vPRoh0R4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The responder advises that protecting downstream devices with GFCI is optional and may be avoided when ground-fault protection is unnecessary.

## Common question patterns
- "Why were the conductors or equipment identified with unusual markings?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Why were the circuit conductors not labeled or numbered for identification and maintenance?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Why do the conductor insulation colors shown in the installation not follow standard color identification?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why was a black conductor used instead of a red conductor for the hot leg?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why was blue tape used to identify the conductor instead of obtaining red-insulated cable or using red tape?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why was tape applied using those colors instead of the expected colors?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why was the neutral conductor not properly identified or marked?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Why was the white conductor not re-identified as an ungrounded conductor?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "I'm no electrician, just a homeowner. You said you used blue tape because you didn't have any red-shielded cable. Why not hit up an electrical supply shop and get the right material? Or, why didn't you use red tape instead of blue?" (V:ZQOTvsXtrKo) (Q:UgydJ41wW2MY5wqWNNB4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Correction): The accepted reply indicates that for split-phase service there is no NEC requirement to mark either hot leg; only the neutral (white) and equipment grounding conductor (green/bare) must be identified. Using red identification tape is a matter of practice, not a mandatory requirement for hot conductors in this configuration.

Q: "Why aren’t your wires marked for what room they go to or what they control" (V:LdNuJksviTY) (Q:Ugy8AADVuDFzNjSRYlB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction): The solution indicates conductor identification is provided on the wire ends and installers transfer those identification tags onto the conductor tails at panelboard breaker terminations for checkout and neat external appearance.

Q: "Nice pulling head.... but blue tape? Wasteful" (V:VHNRHKVVClw) (Q:UgwTf3VTLNVkfPZwFh94AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report): The solution is to use duct tape or standard black vinyl electrical tape for wrapping pulling heads; blue tape was used only due to availability.

Q: "Where is your RED wire?" (V:Frt0vJ4k15g) (Q:Ugyg-AkqawBPq0ce4p54AaABAg)
A (Prescription): Black conductor was used as the hot. The reply asserts that conductor color can be substituted for the hot leg.

Q: "So is a 14/3 wire the one to use for switches and bulbs, and a 14/2 used for outlets? I’m rewriting some things in an old house and all they have is white and black wires ran to bulbs, switches and outlets" (V:KnqMJeNN1ug) (Q:UgzDJ4blztUrqIlSoNB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Code or authority citation): Use 14/3 or 12/3 when a third conductor is required (switch loops, switched half-hot duplex, MWBCs, or travelers); use 14/2 or 12/2 for standard hot-neutral runs. Observe conductor ampacity: 14 AWG on 15 A circuits and 12 AWG on 20 A circuits (per NEC conductor ampacity rules).

Q: "Would of been easier to run pvc conduit …" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:Ugw-e-GzzZOynVkoa6x4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Explanation, Correction): The reply states PVC is often prohibited by fire codes because it can melt, collapse onto occupants and firefighters, and produce hazardous off-gassing during fires.

Q: "Why are the pipes and the box made of metal? Here in the Netherlands we use pvc for pipes and boxes." (V:rvUlnrCuzew) (Q:UgxtUXFpPMs7FLci1r54AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): Use metallic conduit and metal boxes in commercial/industrial installations for enhanced mechanical protection and reliable equipment grounding/bonding. When metallic raceways are impractical, specify impact-resistant PVC or Horcaliet nonmetallic conduit.

Q: "Excellent demonstration and thank you for that. But... I'm seriously concerned with the weakening of the studs by cutting holes in the middle of them to run the pipe. So for a place where aesthetics doesn't matter much s.a. shed, why not r…" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:UgwKtPzfiaJccCxToYJ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Maintain a minimum 5/8 in edge clearance and keep bored holes to no more than 40% of stud depth. If preferred, run exposed EMT/FMC on the surface and secure per conduit support/fastening requirements.

## Common question patterns
- "Is neat, organized panelboard wiring preferable to sloppy or tangled wiring?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Is neat wiring preferable to disorganized wiring?" (asked by 2 commenters)

- "What device could replace a conventional panelboard?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "What is the benefit of a separate 110 panel? Wouldn’t one 110/220 inside be better?" (V:xTpl7WYMkcA) (Q:UgyFtCD7n5iGUDYSLFF4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Install an interior subpanel to expand breaker capacity, centralize generator/critical circuits, shorten homeruns, and place AFCI/GFCI and smart breakers in conditioned space to reduce nuisance trips and longevity issues.

Q: "It's a commercial setting with split-phase instead of 3-phase? Wow." (V:ZQOTvsXtrKo) (Q:Ugz3hm6m7JV5V8pIZs94AaABAg)
A (Explanation, Code or authority citation): Correct, phase configuration is determined by connected load and equipment requirements. Service type, meterbase, and conductor sizing must follow NEC load calculations and ampacity provisions.

Q: "My panel is a Cutler Hammer but I cannot seem to find breakers of that brand and no one can seem to tell me definitively what brand is compatible. Any thoughts?" (V:bGZVILwbyLo) (Q:UgxzxQggbDgmjM8H0n54AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Identifies Cutler-Hammer as Eaton and specifies Eaton CH-series breakers as the compatible breaker family, using brown housings and yellow handles as visual identification.

Q: "Does that specific ModBus have 3 CT clamps for 3 phase or is it connected to Single Phase but with two CT Clamps and the Third CT clamp was left off?" (V:dvbU85ljGH8) (Q:UgynSv3CJQexBEMOfkN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The responder confirms a single‑phase configuration with two CT clamps (PV and grid). The battery inverter/charger uses those CT measurements via the Modbus meter for net‑flow demand signalling and off‑peak charge control.

Q: "Hey man I am new to the channel. I'm 19 currently going to school for business and quite frankly I'm sick of it. Sick of giving all the money I make for some useless degree and desk work is simply not for me. I'm interested in becoming an…" (V:74uD2_Rtv8I) (Q:Ugw4ri2iSVRE57lcmKx4AaABAg)

A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Bond the service neutral at the first means of disconnect; downstream panelboards must have isolated neutral buses and dedicated equipment grounding conductors per the 2020 NEC.

A (Prescription, Correction): The consensus solution is full panelboard/service equipment replacement rather than installing aftermarket breakers, due to compatibility, listing, and AHJ/insurance acceptance concerns.

Q: "Your standby system is open transition or closed transition?" (V:_IDluE3fEoc) (Q:UgzQo7lt8bD-pGVyAld4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The reply confirms the system uses an open-transition automatic transfer switch (break-before-make). The ATS briefly disconnects the load from one source before connecting the other.

Q: "Would be interested in seeing how well other wire connections like the Wago Lever-nuts work. Try running 20 amps through each connection with 12 gauge wire and take their temperature. Then try 30 amps." (V:9hlo87E_GdQ) (Q:UgzuUotXlqjxXp9KPSh4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): Use only UL-listed lever-type connectors for building electrical; avoid non-listed consumer parts. Only a small number of manufacturers produce legitimately listed connector products.

Q: "0:38 Is there contact between the wire and the connector other than that piece of metal that is moved by the lever? If not, Twisting the wires and applying a wire nut seems like it would provide more contact area -- and less heating of the…" (V:9hlo87E_GdQ) (Q:UgzC_tzhW1tXMjrGP6J4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): The respondent recommends Wago lever nuts despite marginally higher contact resistance, arguing the resistance is negligible (comparable to a short length of 2.5 mm^2 conductor) and offers reliable, repeatable connections.

Q: "Does no one use a wire pull grip with fish tape? That us a huge waste of electrical tape where a wire grip is reusable." (V:Frt0vJ4k15g) (Q:UgxZvgefEUfVTbV5_O14AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The consensus recommends that a reusable wire pull grip is a valid pulling accessory but tape is still used to smooth and secure the conductor bundle. For occasional DIY pulls, buyers may opt not to purchase a grip due to infrequent use.

Q: "How other than a pigtail would you remedy this situation?" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:Ugxl7Yn6RJkz6H8zpbN4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction): The practical solution implemented was to pigtail the conductors and shorten/organize the conductor tails to reduce box fill and relieve mechanical strain on the device; no full rewiring was performed.

A (Prescription, Explanation, Correction): Use the correct cutting tool for the intended conductor/task; substituting bolt cutters sacrifices intended application and can produce poor results or damage. In emergencies a substitute may work, but it’s suboptimal for conductor integrity.

Q: "So why own the wirecutters if the bolt cutters do everything the wire cutters can do and then some without risk of damage?" (V:8sO2MOQWh8U) (Q:UgwJY77tvcDR1-MiKpR4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Use wire cutters for soft conductors (copper and aluminum) to obtain clean cuts and protect cutting edges; reserve bolt cutters for steel and other hard materials to avoid dulling delicate cutters.

Q: "Excellent video. Can I use a hammer drill instead of a demo hammer?" (V:vAD3r_nF6L4) (Q:Ugyw1vZZtdg_RJPycnV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Correction): Recommends using water to soften the soil and repeated push/pull cycles, finishing by driving the grounding rod with a sledge hammer when it becomes anchored. This offers a practical alternative to a demolition hammer for rod installation.

Q: "How about a reaming tool" (V:A0cXKa4Y3do) (Q:Ugx8y95CxZxGgT9uUpR4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Experience report): Hand tools (channel locks, linesman pliers, diagonal cutters) are viable for incidental deburring. For repetitive conduit work, carrying a larger channel lock or a dedicated reaming tool improves productivity and consistency.

## Common question patterns
- "Should pigtail connections or through-wiring using receptacle terminals be used?" (asked by 5 commenters)
- "Can 12-2 or 12-3 cable be used for a fan and light circuit?" (asked by 3 commenters)
- "Should receptacles be wired continuously or with separate cable runs?" (asked by 2 commenters)
- "Can a ceiling fan replace a light fixture on the branch circuit?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Are garage boxes home-run or daisy-chained?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Which lighting-circuit wiring method should be used?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Should 14/3 cable be used for travelers or receptacles?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Should a switch loop or dedicated switch conductors be used?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "What if you ran 5 GFI outlets all chained together?instead of just the first one with regular outlets down stream? Would runningall GFI outlets cause that series to trip really easy?.." (V:Uop79H_iqoQ) (Q:Ugx3bZpZBQ3kg22zMpZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation, Experience report): Recommended solution: avoid series line-to-load GFCI daisy chains. Instead, supply each GFCI from the same line feed (parallel line-to-line) so each device only monitors its local load, reducing nuisance trips.

Q: "Very informative thanks. As a UK electrician Im curious to see how things are done across the pond. Couple of questions: I know dryers and stoves are 240v circuits, what about clothes washers or dishwashers? If they are 120v do they typica…" (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:Ugy_rtgMlAkl04sk1mx4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription): For unknown-load convenience receptacles the NEC uses 180 VA per receptacle; on a 120 V 20 A branch circuit (80% continuous limit to 16 A) that equates to ten receptacles. Dedicated appliances require branch-circuit sizing per NEC and may need individual dedicated circuits.

Q: "Are pigtails the best way to add a receptacle in the middle of a circuit?" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:UgwEX0Dz3i1MkK6TQHV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Both through-wiring (pass-through) and pigtail splices are code-compliant if conductor length, conductor ampacity, and receptacle device ratings are respected. Use pigtails when terminations are difficult, when multiple cables are present, or when GFCI/AFCI or MWBC wiring requires dedicated connections.

Q: "Great Video! Could you use 12-2 wire for the switch instead of 12-3?" (V:1D5OqJ5SF_I) (Q:UgwV_W7qE9NMQUvHE_B4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Use 12-2 when a single switched hot is sufficient; use 12-3 to provide an additional switched conductor for separate fan/light control or 3-way switching. Running 12-3 is recommended for spare conductor provisioning.

Q: "Why is this made out of metal and not something non conductive?" (V:rvUlnrCuzew) (Q:UgwUJEdLZKzwr-tHh_J4AaABAg)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "I had my house's electrical panel replaced, but the electrical company that did the work replaced the 115 amp CBs with 20 amp breakers. I called the company and was told it was OK with that. It does not sound correct to me. What do you thi…" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgzqBeSRKKC1hACllE54AaABAg)
A (Correction, Code or authority citation, Prescription): The reply indicates the 20 A breakers are oversized for 14 AWG conductors; per NEC 240.4(D) 14 AWG conductors are limited to 15 A. Remediate by installing 15 A overcurrent protection or upgrade the conductors to 12 AWG.

Q: "What is I have a 20 amp from the braker n use large wire and connect it to a 15 amp outlet ?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:Ugxl8JWp5I-l-Ib7PhB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): Match overcurrent protection, conductor ampacity, and device rating, use a 20 A-rated receptacle on a 20 A circuit. Do not place a 15 A device on a 20 A-protected branch per NEC device coordination principles.

Q: "I recently replaced some old outlets for some new outlets that said “14 wire only” but connected old 12 wire to it. Is that okay or should I switch them out?" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgxHqMRWlcveLdtITql4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Replace the receptacle with a 20 A-rated device matched to 12 AWG conductors and ensure the overcurrent device is 20 A. Device rating must match branch-circuit ampacity (NEC 210.21).

Q: "I found that my garage has 15 amp breakers. Should they not be 20 amps instead? Seems like you might want to run some high-powered power tools in there." (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:Ugw4LYiB6W-E1vWLeQd4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): The responder explains breaker rating must match conductor ampacity: 14 AWG requires 15 A protection, and to have 20 A circuits you must install 12 AWG conductors. This aligns with NEC overcurrent protection principles.

## Common question patterns
- "Is bonding the HF station busbar to the home's electrical panel over a long run an appropriate grounding arrangement for the amplifier?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is bonding the neutral and ground bus bars in my enclosure correct and necessary to address an inadequate grounding connection?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is connecting a shower's grounding conductor only to a ground rod safe and compliant when the user feels current while operating the shower?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is connecting the battery negative to the aluminum boat hull an acceptable grounding or return arrangement?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is connecting the inverter chassis ground to the house-battery negative terminal correct when the starter and house battery systems have separate protection?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is connecting the outboard negative conductor directly to the battery negative terminal, rather than the negative bus bar, acceptable?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Has this electrical container been properly earthed?" (asked by 1 commenters)
- "Is installing a second bonded neutral bus to terminate the capped air-conditioning neutral conductor acceptable?" (asked by 1 commenters)

## Example questions and answers
Q: "I have a sub panel being fed w old circle wire 8x3 BX (not woven cloth) no separate ground…I know the sheathing acts as a ground but should I be concerned? It controls 3 bedrooms, bath and attic." (V:B0XyDf0o-Vw) (Q:Ugxdum1Wdj241EWIbAZ4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): The replies advise bringing the subpanel into compliance by providing an isolated equipment grounding conductor and separating neutrals and grounds. Also verify whether the BX sheath qualifies as an equipment grounding conductor per NEC 250.118 and ensure proper, secure terminations.

Q: "Would someone be exposed to receiving an electric shock if he or she touches the metal enclousure of a load? or Could we assume that the installation continues to be safe since the neutral and EGC are linked together at one point (MBJ)? Wh…" (V:LhZcWykPWQc) (Q:UgxO2OIaYMCPUo3csTZ4AaABAg)
A (Correction, Explanation, Code or authority citation): The responder concludes it is hazardous: an energized enclosure with insufficient fault current can allow a person to complete the circuit and be shocked. They emphasize that grounding conductor sizing and Code-required installation affect safe operation.

Q: "Hi. I only have the black and white wires with a copper wire. Would that ground still work if I’m swapping out a new dish washer or do I have to re-do the grounding to the black/white and green cord that’s on the new dish washer?" (V:ttun_X7JIAM) (Q:Ugy2vPzMcCrTwqqzAPx4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Bond the appliance green grounding conductor to the uninsulated copper EGC or to the junction-box grounding screw, and connect black to hot and white to neutral. This provides the required equipment bonding per NEC 250.

Q: "The other day I had to reset a circuit breaker and noticed that for one string of outlets the neutral wire was connected to the ground bar while all other white wires were connected to the neutral bar. Everything seems to work just fine, b…" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:Ugz-_KE63oMLBhQW4yV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): If the termination is at the service equipment/main panel the neutral-to-ground bond is permitted. At a subpanel, neutrals must be isolated from equipment grounding conductors per NEC requirements.

Q: "do you have any video of what a bonding wire from the electrical panel to a cold water copper pipe should look like? Or if it would be easier, I could send you a short video of my house set up if you could tell me what is wrong with it." (V:hEDto-bnHKw) (Q:UgyoymKL6v7ieiJPBL94AaABAg)

A (Prescription, Explanation): The battery can pay back if the household shifts loads to daytime solar generation or charges from cheap off‑peak tariffs for later use. If most consumption already occurs during generation, the battery provides little additional economic value.

A (Prescription, Experience report): The provided solution indicates the 4 kW inverter is adequate for common van loads but is undersized for continuous air conditioning; sustained HVAC operation requires roughly 10 kW.

## Example questions and answers
Q: "I had an outlet for a kitchen stove but got rid of the stove, and wanted to use the breaker/wire to install a 30A RV outlet. The breaker is (2) 120v, 30a breakers attached together with a plastic piece. The guy I had install the outlet did…" (V:4Xq8dddqxw8) (Q:UgzCxUx5E8f8KHAHTzB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Code or authority citation, Correction): Replace the handle-tied/tandem configuration with a proper single-pole 30 A breaker (or otherwise correct breaker configuration) to comply with NEC and avoid inspection rejection.

Q: "I have a garage outlet GFCI it has 2 white and 2 black lines coming in and pigtailed to line side of GFCI. Then load side had only one black one white. I know the GFCI load side goes to a chain of outlets inside the house. I wanted to chai…" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:Ugydr_gocnAwN315zDl4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Tap/pigtail the GFCI load side to extend GFCI protection to additional receptacles; connecting to the line side leaves downstream receptacles unprotected. Uninsulated EGCs are acceptable in a metal box.

Q: "Did it pass inspection? You have a 15 amp GFI on a 20 amp breaker... that won't pass." (V:gJ75hYJYLb8) (Q:UgwhcaMGTYTf2qNjfY54AaABAg)
A (Experience report, Code or authority citation): The installer reported the temporary service passed inspection. Other responders contest code interpretation regarding a 15 A GFCI on a 20 A circuit.

Q: "I would like to put a GFCI in the bathroom, but I don't know how to do it without a proper ground wire. Secondly, that same circuit feeds three bedrooms. ... I see that using pigtails to bypass the load on the GFCI would work. But is there…" (V:K3RIjUnrNTQ) (Q:UgxnmtlKdfSRU7hwrqV4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Explanation): Solution: pigtail the branch feeding the bathroom and attach the bathroom feed to the GFCI line terminals only so downstream bedrooms are not load-side protected. GFCIs sense imbalance between hot and neutral (~5 mA) and will provide protection without an equipment grounding conductor.

A (Prescription, Code or authority citation): Install a GFCI receptacle and label it 'No Equipment Ground' to comply with NEC where no equipment grounding conductor exists. Alternatively, run a new equipment grounding conductor or provide proper bonding to the metal box for a grounded installation.

Q: "I have a 3-way switch next to a single pole in a 2 gang wall plate. The 3 way is wired as expected, line, traveller, common, then the line is jumped to the single switch. The single switch had load from the fixture and line with that jump…" (V:syaGf_XUMxA) (Q:UgzwT0GdoZrKHgtURAZ4AaABAg)

A (Prescription, Correction): The reply advises using a separate/dedicated branch circuit for the receptacle rather than tapping the light circuit to avoid inadvertent switch control.

Q: "Is it wrong to connect my light from the socket which has 2.5mm cables and how safe is my bulb if I don't connect the earth wire" (V:2tdN85reWN0) (Q:Ugw32hwzmiVNhyP02hB4AaABAg)
A (Prescription, Referral): The recommended solution is to feed lighting circuits from the consumer unit and use 1.5 mm² conductors for lighting; the replier also advises consulting a professional electrician.

Q: "Why didn't you just leave the existing receptacle and add the new one? Would have been less work." (V:Jpu-3zB8Pqs) (Q:Ugx1hbpmGvfSDaPnqYR4AaABAg)
A (Code or authority citation, Prescription, Explanation): The NEC regulates branch-circuit load rather than a fixed receptacle count. For bathrooms, provide the required 20 A branch circuit and GFCI protection while verifying conductor ampacity, box fill, and grounding/bonding.

Q: "Why not use a big pull box, then run a few conduits for the main panel. This allows for clean and future work (if needed)." (V:l-gOTyql6RM) (Q:Ugx_i0eD988iIJQBvzB4AaABAg)
